speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
On behalf of the Prime Minister I should like to inform the house of the arrival in Canada of Prime Minister Curtin of Australia. Mr. Curtin reached this country this afternoon, and will arrive in Ottawa this evening from Montreal at 10.10 p.m. As hon. members may know, and will be glad to know, Mrs. Curtin, who accompanied Prime Minister Curtin from Australia to Washington, arrived in Ottawa earlier to-day.
Arrangements have been made for Mr. Curtin to address members of this house and of the senate on Thursday afternoon. It is my understanding that Mr. Curtin's address on that occasion will be broadcast so that all the citizens of Canada may have the privilege of hearing him.
It is proposed that when the house adjourns this evening the formal session will stand adjourned until four o'clock on Thursday, but it is anticipated that the members will assemble at the usual hour of three o'clock without going into formal session so that they may have the privilege of hearing, along with the members of the senate, the address of Mr. Curtin.
I am sure that I am speaking for all members of the house, and for the country generally, when I say that to us Mr. and Mrs. Curtin represent a sister dominion whose progress in peace and whose prowess in war have been a matter of pride and admiration on the part of the whole of the British commonwealth of nations. Therefore we feel particularly happy to welcome these two distinguished people on this occasion.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I just say in connection with the words which have been uttered by the acting leader of the government that the high standing of the Right Hon. Mr. Curtin and the nation which he represents will ensure for him and Mrs. Curtin a royal welcome while he is in Canada. We hope that our hospitality will know no bounds, while they are here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF DOCTOR PENFIELD AS TO SPECIAL CENTRES FOR NEUROLOGICAL TREATMENT
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, of which I have given notice, in view of the statement made yesterday by Doctor Wilder G. Penfield, leading neurological surgeon on the North American continent and head of the Montreal Neurological Institute, who is reported in the Gazette of to-day to the effect that the offer to the government of the institute as a treatment centre had been turned down because of fear of the establishment of an embarrassing precedent. Doctor Penfield further said:
It is not for us to question this decision, but four and a half years of this war have now passed, and the Canadian government has done practically nothing to establish special centres for the care of war injuries of the nervous system; nothing at all in Quebec and the maritimes.
I would ask the minister to inform the house why this offer was not accepted.
3364	COMMONS
Armed Forces-Neurological Treatment
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health):	I received
notice of my hon. friend's question just before I came into the house, and hurriedly perused the article in the Montreal Gazette. Of course, as Your Honour is aware, it is entirely improper to quote from press reports on the orders of the day, though I am not making any point of that. Two statements are made in the article in question, the first having' to do with the lack of accommodation for the armed services. This statement is entirely inaccurate. At the present time we are operating 23,000 hospital beds in Canada, 15,000 by the armed services. In 1939 the Department of Pensions and National Health was operating 2,700 beds; at the present time it is operating 8,450 and will be operating 10,000 within a year.
In regard to neurological cases, I have the most profound admiration for Doctor Penfield, as one of the outstanding men of the world in his field; but in conjunction with the armed services we recently established four centres for the special care of neurological cases, in Edmonton, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Toronto. In Montreal neurological cases receive preliminary investigation at Ste. Anne's and are then moved to the Montreal Neurological Institute for major surgery.
With reference to the alleged turning down of the institute, I take it that my hon. friend's question refers to a suggestion that was made for an additional wing to that institute for the special care of such cases. This is exactly the sort of suggestion that was received in five, six or seven hundred similar cases all over Canada, from other hospitals, which in the very nature of things cannot be accepted. I can assure my hon. friend that every possible consideration has been given, is being given and will be given to the treatment and care of neurological cases in the armed forces of the crown before and after discharge.

subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF DOCTOR PENFIELD AS TO SPECIAL CENTRES FOR NEUROLOGICAL TREATMENT
speechtext: Does the minister not think a man with the outstanding ability of Doctor Penfield should be given an opportunity of doing this work in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF DOCTOR PENFIELD AS TO SPECIAL CENTRES FOR NEUROLOGICAL TREATMENT
speechtext:
I do not believe that question is in order, either. I said I had the most profound admiration for a man of the outstanding ability of Doctor Penfield, but he displayed a remarkable lack of knowledge of the preparations made both by the armed services and by the Department of Pensions and National Health in regard to the care of neurological cases in Canada. We are using his services now.
(Mr. Bruce.]

How many employees are working under the wartime prices and trade board? How many offices are there across Canada; how many employees are there on the inspection staff, and how many are on loan to this branch of the service?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As at March 31, 1944, there were 5,112 employees. These are paid employees. There are fourteen regional offices and about 114 or 115 local offices.
How many are employed as inspectors?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have not that information at the moment but I will make a note of the question and get it later. In order that I may be clear as to what is meant, does my hon. friend mean enforcement inspectors or some other type of inspector?
I think it is the enforcement inspectors. There are a great many of them travelling all across the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised there are between three and four hundred.

How many young lawyers are employed?

War Appropriation-Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information.
All the young lawyers in the country are working for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We will get that information.

Mr. Chairman, each year in the town in which I reside a poultry fair is held. A large amount of dressed poultry is brought in; as a matter of fact in two days last December the producers brought in ninety tons of fresh poultry. There was practically an army of wartime prices and trade board inspectors there at the same time. To my knowledge there were nine of them, and how many more I do not know. The point I am raising this afternoon has not so much to do with the inspectors as it has with the controls placed upon the poultry producers of that community. On those particular days wartime prices and trade board inspectors placed blackboards in the market square advising the buyers what the ceiling prices were at which they could buy poultry. In my estimation they were working exactly backward. A farmer would come in with a load of poultry that might grade A or B, and he was told definitely by the inspectors that he could not accept more than 30i cents for chickens and 351 cents for turkeys, the idea being that the poultry must be sold ungraded. Another farmer might drive in alongside the first man with a load of poultry that would not grade more than C or D. If the buyers saw fit they could pay him the same price because his poultry was also ungraded. From talking to the buyers I know that they were anxious to pay the producer considerably more than they were allowed to pay. A lot of the dressed poultry taken out of that town in those two or three days was shipped to Montreal or Toronto by truck and sold in the stores in those cities at a price of 43 cents for grade A and 42 cents for grade B. My contention is that the farmers were robbed of from 7 to 8 cents per pound due to the way in which the wartime prices and trade board handled the situation. I am protesting against that kind of thing. The men who purchased these fowl were willing to pay more than they were allowed to pay, and the result was that they were able to make an exorbitant profit of from 10 to 13 cents per pound, a profit entirely out of line with what the producer received.
I have no axe to grind about the price ceiling to the consumer. I think that is perfectly all right, but I protest against a price ceiling to the producer which is 13 cents below what the consumer has to pay. That is out of all proportion. My contention is that the ceiling to the consumer should be enforced, but

instead of the wartime prices and trade board saying to the producers of these fowl, "You cannot receive more than 30J cents for your chickens or more than 35| cents for your turkeys," they should say to the buyers, "You cannot pay less than those prices." If the large concerns that are buying this poultry are satisfied to take a smaller profit than 10 to 15 cents a pound, then I say they should be allowed to do so.
In my estimation this practice is doing much to discourage agriculture in this country. On the one side we have the government urging the farmer to produce more and, on the other, we have the wartime prices and trade board doing much to discourage that which is being requested by other branches of government. I felt it my duty to bring this matter to the attention of the department and to urge that this thing be not repeated. The order should be amended so that the farmer who is doing the work, who is producing at the request of certain branches of government, will receive a fair price. There should not be the spread between what is paid to the farmer and what the consumer pays as exists in this case.

What
authority did these inspectors have to take the stand they did?

I think what the hon. member has just said should be considered. Fowl should be properly graded. At the present *time we are carrying on an extensive business in bootlegging and it ought to be controlled.

Who are
"we"?
Poultry should be classified and graded so that the buyer knows exactly what he is buying. That would regulate prices. I think perhaps the farmer is being legislated against in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to deal with the points raised by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox. There are three ceilings on poultry, as I have no doubt my hon. friend knows. There is a ceiling on the wholesale price, there is a ceiling on the producer and there is a ceiling to the retail trade. The producer of poultry is entitled to sell at the ceiling price according to who is his customer. If he sells to a wholesaler, he gets the producer price; if he sells to a retailer, he gets the wholesale price, and if he sells to you or to me as consumers, he gets the retail consumer price. That is the price ceiling policy with respect to dressed poultry.
As to what these inspectors were doing in my hon. friend's town, I must confess that I have no personal information. I am not an

War Appropriation-Finance
expert in the grading of poultry. The wartime prices and trade board has nothing to do with establishing the grades of dressed poultry; that is done either by the provincial agricultural authorities or by those of the federal government. In any case the grades are fixed and the prices board establishes ceilings for the different grades.

What
authority had these men to step in?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: 'Would my hon. friend tell me about what time of the year it was?
It was December 3 or 4.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I asked one of my officials and he said just before Christmas there was a considerable-

Possibly I did not make myself clear. I am not finding any fault with the grading of the poultry, but the poultry which was brought into the market square on these particular days, unless it comes through the pool, is not graded. Last year the pool did not function and none of the poultry brought into the market was graded. The farmer is not allowed to grade the poultry himself, and there were no inspectors from the Department of Agriculture there to grade it. The result was that every farmer was forced to sell the poultry at the ungraded price, no matter how good or how poor it was. That is what I am complaining of.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of the particular facts my hon. friend is bringing forward. I take it that this poultry, turkeys, fowl or whatever it was, for some reason or other had to be sold as ungraded poultry and was therefore subject to the ceiling for ungraded poultry.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked, as to the authority for the inspectors doing what they were doing. I am not clear as to what orders they were enforcing, but I am advised that just prior to Christmas of last year there was a considerable tendency on the part of certain buyers in cities and elsewhere to push up the prices without too much regard for the ceiling, and that the enforcement division were instructed to keep their eyes open for that sort of thing.
But that does not take care of the situation. What determined the price when the fowl was ungraded?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have not the order before me, but I am advised that under the order there is a price ceiling for ungraded poultry.

No matter what may be the quality of the poultry?
100-212J

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quite so.

That just illustrates once more the fact that when you set up regulations to interfere with the laws of supply and demand, as is being done by the wartime prices and trade board, great irregularities and injustices are bound to occur. Here is a man with grade A poultry, and he is told by the so-called gestapo that he cannot get the price for grade A poultry, that he must take the ungraded poultry price. I am satisfied that the regulations were made with good intent; I want to make that clear; but it is the operation of these regulations that brings about injustices and great discontent in this country. Make no mistake about it-the hand of every man who produces is against these regulations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Not the hand of every
consumer.
I am talking about the producers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I know you are.

The producer has to have somebody stand up for him once in a while. The consumers of this country are not to be so greatly pitied. With a national income of ten billion dollars they have money enough to pay and are willing to pay, but I do agree that we should endeavour to keep prices within reasonable ranges. How do these regulations work? Here is another perfect illustration of the inflexibility of the rules and regulations laid down here in Ottawa by a group of white-collared boys who never were in the poultry business, who know nothing about it, but who sit around a table and draft a lot of regulations without knowing how the thing is going to work out, without knowing how it is going to affect both the producer and the consumer. That is what I object to, and that is what the people of this country are objecting to. The regulations are so inflexible, and then those who are administering them hold the fear of fine and imprisonment over the people. That is the kind of thing the people are rebelling against to-day, and this government will find it out when they go to the polls. I do not know anything that is going to drive this government out of power quicker than the way in which these regulations are administered. I am sure I am right. I can run my whole campaign in the next election if I want to on this very question, and I will be elected.
I too.

The regulations are drafted with good intent. I am not questioning the idea behind the scheme,
War App ropria t ion-Finance

although I have often said that at the beginning prices were frozen on a very uneven scale. I illustrate that by the freezing of the price of hay in my province at the October, 1941, price. Anybody who knows anything about hay, and we produce a good deal of hay in our part of the country, knows that October is the month when hay is at its lowest price level. That is just after the new crop has been pressed. The price of hay rises steadily from October to April, and the thrifty farmer, if he can, holds his hay until he can get the top price in April. But the price of hay was fixed by the prices board at the lowest price for hay, the October price. That is the price the farmer had to accept for his hay in the month of April, when the price ordinarily rises to its peak. The farmer will never forget it. That is the indictment that I make against these regulations. They are so inflexible. They are like the laws of the Medes and Persians. These bureaucrats are like the Bourbons; they never learn anything. They did not know anything to start with, and they never learn anything as they go along. They are never in touch with local conditions-
And they never ask any member of parliament for advice.

No, they never ask any member of parliament. I could have told them about hay. That is one thing I happen to know because in days gone by, on lands owned by me, I produced a great deal of baled hay. I was fortunate enough to get out of that market with the coming of the automobile, and I am glad I did. But hay is coming back into its own now, with all the restrictions on gasoline. Hay is a real commodity now in the Saint John valley.
Does the prices board ever ask anybody about the local conditions? Take the case mentioned by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox. There is a case where the farmer was robbed of seven cents a pound on his grade A poultry, and it was done because of government regulations which do not have regard to actualities. How does the parliamentary assistant defend that sort of thing? I know he is not personally responsible; it is the administrative officers who are responsible for that sort of thing.
I want to ask a question about salaries. You have nine and a half million dollars here for salaries, and the board has about five thousand employees scattered all over the country. That is an average of about 81,900 each. What is the ranges of salaries paid? How much does the chairman get? What does the secretary get? What is the number of employees in the high income group? The country would like to know what this organiza-
tion is costing them and what it is costing the producers, because they are being kept down although they are still taxpayers. I also want to know how many lawyers the board has. It has engaged lawyers to conduct prosecutions from time to time. I am not objecting to prosecutions for infractions of the regulations, but my observation is that the employment of these prosecuting attorneys in my part of the country is a form of political patronage. I know it is so in my county, and I am told it is so everywhere. I had someone look up for me the names of the lawyers in New Brunswick who were prosecuting infractions of these regulations. Would you believe it, there is only one lone Tory engaged to prosecute in the province; he is in the county of Charlotte, and the only reason he was appointed was that there is not a Liberal lawyer left in the county because they had all been given jobs. There are not many of them there in any event. The fact remains that only one Conservative lawyer in New Brunswick was employed by this board. I want to know how these lawyers are appointed and what their fees are. Are they appointed through the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

That is
what I thought. They are on the patronage list of the Department of Justice? Correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would not know about
that.

Well, you could easily find out. I think the minister, perhaps, does know something about this. I make the statement that I believe there is a patronage list established in the expending of this money, which is voted under the guise of war, to pay Liberal lawyers, some of whom ought to be in the army. I am not going to name them. I understand that they are patriots to the extent of $25, $35, $50 a day, prosecuting infractions of this act. I should like to have a break-down of the employees in categories, and I want full information about the employment of the lawyers-what they are paid, how they are paid and who fixes their remuneration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First of all I would like to deal with my hon. friend's remarks as to the price ceiling policy. He said in connection with these agricultural prices that ceilings were fixed by a bunch of white-collar boys here in Ottawa. I just want to point out to him that the person mainly responsible for fixing these agricultural prices is the administrator of meat and poultry, Mr. F. S. Grisdale, who, as my hon. friend knows, is a former minister of agriculture of Alberta and the head

War Appropriation-Finance
of an agricultural college, and who can hardly be described as a *white-collar boy who knows very little about prices.
He is not a dirt farmer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In addition he avails himself, and so do the officers of the board, of the assistance of officials of the Department of Agriculture.
As to the criticism of the fixing of the price ceiling on hay, I am advised that hay has been exempt from the price ceiling since the early days of the controls.
It was exempted after a roar went up from one end of the Saint John valley to the other.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The price ceiling was imposed in November, 1941.
October.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And hay was exempted from the price ceiling, I am advised, in December, 1941.

That is
after they made the mistake.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A ceiling was placed on hay in the western provinces in November of 1943; I think in British Columbia, at the request of the provincial agricultural authorities, because the price was running up too fast.
That just shows a system of trial and error.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As to the question of salaries, I can get my hon. friend the break-down which he asks. He will remember, not I think this session but in the last session, questions were asked-one, I know, by the hon. member for Lake Centre-as to the number of officials of the board in certain salary categories. That answer was given; it involved a considerable amount of *work; and I wonder if my hon. friend would be satisfied if I have the officials of the board check to see if there is any substantial variation from that return, which was tabled, I think, towards the latter part of last session. I doubt if there has been; but if he insists on the information, of course we can obtain it.

Mr, ABBOTT:	Perhaps my hon. friend

In reference to grading of poultry, as to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury seems to be so terribly concerned, I wonder whether in the cases he has in mind the producers themselves have not been somewhat at fault. Certainly the officials of the wartime prices and trade board would have nothing to do in the matter of grading, and if control is to be exercised as far as the consumer and the producer are concerned we must have some basis. If we are to have ceiling prices we would naturally have those prices established, or ought to, according to grade.	[DOT]

How can you?
Mr. WARREN i If they are graded, why not? What is to hinder establishing ceiling prices according to grade?
What if there is no possibility of having grading?

Well then, whose fault is it? I do not know. In the village of Eganville, near which I live, a number of years ago we marketed our poultry and eggs in the usual haphazard manner. The federal Department of Agriculture, I believe, initiated this scheme. A young fellow was established in a very small office, some of the farmers got together and put up their notes as collateral, and this young man started in grading eggs, having first been trained by an official of the Department of Agriculture. For the first year or two that young man was operating the plant the business was very small, but over a period of just a few years it has developed to a matter of $100,000 or more a year. One advantage of this young man having been trained was that when he graded a crate of eggs that grade was accepted on any market. That was not true if a merchant graded the eggs; his eggs would be regraded at Montreal and they might be placed in a different grade from that fixed by the local merchant. In that neighbourhood there has been a gradual but continuous increase in production of poultry and a very marked improvement in quality. In the old days probably not twenty per cent of our poultry were grade A. Now eighty per cent are grade A. The same is true of eggs. Nobody is suffering because of it. The grader instead of working in a place by himself now has a grading machine and a half dozen or more helpers around him. In the fall of the year the farmers bring in their poultry which are left there, weighed and graded, and there is never much grumbling or dispute that I am aware of, respecting the grading of poultry. In some communities by a little cooperative

effort on the part of the producers what is thought to be a grievance can be very easily corrected.
The same thing is true of the village of Cobden. Within the last few years the grading and handling of poultry and eggs have become big business in that village, and the revenue in those districts must have increased tremendously. Instead of a woman raising say fifty poultry she handles them by the hundreds. The women make a job of it and they know how to dress their poultry. They go around in groups. The neighbours help each other. They find out the. proper methods to use in dressing poultry to have them grade properly. The result is there is not much dissatisfaction. I do not know why we should jump on the wartime prices and trade board officials with respect to grades. If we do not pay for our products according to grade we shall be doing the producers harm instead of good. A man ought to be paid for his products on the basis of quality.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Renfrew North. I am surprised to see him standing in his place and agreeing that the farmer should be cheated out of thirteen cents a pound on those chickens just because he was unable to have them graded. I made it clear a few moments ago that we agreed with grading. So far as producing poultry is concerned, more poultry are produced in my constituency than in any other constituency in Canada. I am not in the least disturbed about any successful contradiction of that statement.
We have had this fair at Napanee for many years and we have followed through the grading of poultry and eggs ever since the commencement of it. But the point I strongly emphasized to the committee was that last December it was impossible for the farmers to get their poultry graded because the Department of Agriculture could not send graders there or did not send them there. It made no difference how good the poultry were, all that the farmer was allowed to accept for them was 30i cents a pound. Those chickens were taken a hundred and fifty miles to Toronto and sold to the consumer at 43 cents a pound for grade A and 42 cents a pound for grade B. I say that should not happen. It is not protecting the farmer. The point I have tried to emphasize is that the inspectors of the wartime prices and trade board were on the market square and when the farmer drove up with his load of poultry it made no difference whether they were grade A. B, C, or D. the inspector walked up to farmer's rig and when the buyer came along the inspector said,

War Appropriation-Finance
"You can pay only 30J cents a pound for those chickens." I say that is dictatorship. Instead of the board saying to the buyer, "You cannot pay more than 301 cents for those chickens," it should protect the consumers who are paying 42 or 43 cents a pound.
In many instances the buyers wanted to pay more for this poultry last fall, but the wartime prices and trade board said it could not be done because the poultry were not graded. Instead of the board saying, "You cannot pay more than 301 cents a pound", they should say, "You cannot pay the farmer less than 301 cents".
Have them graded.

We are ready to accept
grading at all times. That is the way we should like to sell our products. We have done more in our district to improve the quality of poultry and eggs than any other district in Canada. I was amused to hear the hon. member for Renfrew North saying that the farmers in his constituency dealt in hundreds of chickens. In my part of the country they deal in thousands. I have one hatchery alone -that has been producing since the first of February and i;t will be producing until -the end of September. It is producing at the rate of 16,000 per week. I have three hatcheries in my constituency, but this one hatchery is producing 16,000 a week and will continue at that rait-e until the end of September.
I do not want to repeat these things, but I do wish to urge upon the parliamentary assistant to -the minister -the necessity of his seeing to it that the wartime prices and trade board are made acquainted with the difficulties that the farmers had last year, and that the same difficulty does not arise again this fall.

I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Ed-ward-Lennox with respect to the marketing of poultry. I have been convinced from the inception of -price control in this country, as has been pointed out -by other hon. members -to-day, that the primary- producer was -taken at an unfair advantage and a very uneven price structure. We of the opposition have battled continuously for some form of parity for the primary -producer. This applies not only to poultry -but to all primary products of the country. Beef -is a glaring example. Hon. members have taken advantage of every occasion to refer to the difficult situation of beef production in Canada. Beef and hogs and other commodities may come under some other department, but back of all the difficulties is Donald Gordon and his price control administration.
The beef feeder, the man who has been accustomed to finishing beef in Canada, has
been almost entirely -put out of business by price complications and controls. The price of grain to-day and the price of beef do not permit the feeder to b-uy cattle and finish the animal properly as he used to do.
The excuse that is always given to us is that we cannot now take advantage of our natural market to the south because it would be unfair to the consumer of this country. That market is on the average thirty-five per cent higher than it is in this country. The argument has always been advanced in this house by several ministers that in the case of hogs we m-ust supply the finest type to Britain in order to obtain -that market. Surely that same argument ought to apply to beef, but we have not been doing that. We have been shipping cow beef to Britain. True, that has -been -taken off the market recently, but surely we will not retain that market by supplying that -type of cattle to Britain. The set-up is not consistent.
We had a new system of hog grading put in force in recent months in Canada with bonuses for the select hog. I think that is all to the good. But on -the other hand we have controls by -the packers, and penalties which they impose. Under the old schedule up -to March on a heavy hog dressing 220 pounds there was a penalty of some -two cents a pound. This hog is a choice hog in the United States. Under the new set-up which prevails in grading -the settlements, in April -the packer penalized the producer 41 cents a pound on -the heavy hog. There is over twice the penalty -that previously applied on that 220-pound hog. Previously there was a penalty of $4.40. Under the present set-up of settlements on -the first of -the month the producer is penalized $9.35, -through no fault of his own. Besides, man-power enters into it because there was a glut in all of the abattoirs throughout western Canada.
A man with a select hog ready to go on the market was not allowed to market it; the hog became a heavy, and he was further penalized by the packer who took his product; there was no control at all. In addition, a great deal of that heavier pork is sold for domestic consumption in Canada, in many cases at a higher price than is paid for the select bacon by the bacon board. The government does not profess to do anything about that. I say that in many of these matters the price controls are very unfair to the primary producers of this country, who have always received secondary consideration. I have made it plain that I am in favour of price control for the benefit of the consumers, but in connection with many items the consumers have benefited to a far greater extent than the primary producers.

While I am on my feet I should like to ask the hon. gentleman another question. I was not sure of the figure he gave in the breakdown in connection with ration coupon banking. I believe he gave some figure of about $800,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: I believe this is a new venture; previously these coupons were handled on a different basis. I know that gasoline coupons were handled by the oil companies themselves, at no cost whatever to the country. I should like an explanation from the hon. gentleman as to why this change was made and what it cost the government last year to have these coupons handled in this way. I should like to know just what the banks receive for this service, which I understand was performed gratis by other people until this change was made, but which now costs the taxpayers of this country $840,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the earlier days of coupon rationing this service was provided largely by the retailers. It involved a great deal of work and a great deal of additional expense, and it was felt that this was perhaps an unfair burden to impose upon one particular class of the community.
Unless they were paid for it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is perfectly true, but that would involve a very difficult administrative job which probably would result in greater expenditure and less efficiency than is the case under the coupon banking system which has now been introduced, and which I think I am right in saying was adapted from other countries, particularly Great Britain.
Was the voluntary system efficient?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that under the voluntary system there was a considerable clutter-up of coupons and considerable difficulty both on the part of the retailers and on the part of the government in maintaining accurate records.
Was there not also the possibility of fraud?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
And of course there was the obvious danger that the coupons might be handled improperly. This coupon banking system was based upon systems in vogue in other countries, including Great Britain, and the work was placed with the banks. It may be said that the banks should have done it for no'thing, but it was an additional service which the banks were asked to provide. In the case of the retail grocer or merchant, he was

getting the benefit of the rationing system in the sense that there was a reasonable flow of supplies, and he was maintained ini business, but it was purely an extra service as far as the banks were concerned and they are being paid for it on a cost basis.
I do not think the retailer looked upon the rationing system with much favour, because his supplies were kept down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I dare say that is true; but I venture to suggest that the retailer would have looked with much less favour on the absence of rationing in connection with these very short commodities. He accepted the rationing system; he may have considered it an evil, but I believe he recognized that it was necessary, not only to assure equitable distribution to the people but for the protection of his own business. Very briefly that is the reason for this charge in connection with ration coupon banking.
What do you pay the banks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The sum of $460,618.51 has been paid by the government to the chartered banks of Canada for their services in connection with ration coupon banking for the period from March 1, 1943, to November 30, 1943.
Just how is it handled, and what are they paid?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The monthly charges have been running between $55,000 and $65,000. The board's estimate of $840,000 was made prior to the discontinuance of meat rationing and therefore may be in excess of need. However, it is felt that there should be some leeway in the event that other commodities may have to be rationed. The rates the banks are using at present were based on a time study of the actual operations involved, and represent only the banks' direct salary cost and out of pocket expenses in connection with stationery, supplies and so on.
Then they are doing it at cost?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, at cost.
What is the actual rate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It has been running at $55,000 to $65,000 a month.
I know that, but what is the basis of the charge?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The rates are subject to review from time to time both by the board and by the bankers, through the Canadian

War Appropriation-Finance
Bankers' association. They are based on a study of the time of the bank's employees involved in providing these services.
How do you arrive at that figure of $55,000 or $65,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that the figure is arrived at on the banks submitting evidence of the actual time spent by their employees in handling these coupons. It is cleared through the Canadian Bankers' association to the board, and figures are submitted as to the time occupied by the employees of the banks and the amount of stationery, and so on, involved.

So that really you have to take the word of the banks for the whole
thing?
Mr. ABBOTT^ Subject to check by the officers of the board to ascertain whether the statements of the banks as to the time consumed are correct.
Surely the officers of the board know the basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
Do they not get 25 cents in addition for each account?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not on the basis of so much for each coupon, or anything like that. The basis of remuneration to the banks is their actual out-of-pocket expense. That may not be determined to the. last cent, but as closely as it can be arrived at the work is done by the banks on a cost basis.

Just to keep the record straight, not long ago I obtained some information from the department in regard to this very matter, and according to that information the banks were paid 25 cents for every account established in regard to these coupons. I have the letter up in my office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will get more detailed information as to the way in which this is operated, but the general statement I have made is correct; payment to the banks is on the basis of the banks' cost. How that cost is arrived at, other than by the time taken, and so on, I am not in a position to say at the moment, but I will get the information.
The minister's information may be correct as far as the figure of $55,000 a month is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Between $55,000 and $65,000. Let me say at once that this is not business for which the banks asked. They did not invite it at all; the government asked them to undertake it.

That is so. At the same time, if I understand the situation correctly according to the information given to me by the department some time ago, in addition to the actual cost of this operation as far as the time of their employees is concerned-and that is in accordance with information I received-the banks are paid 25 cents for each account they have established.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall verify that. I think there is some misunderstanding there and I shall have to check on that and give an answer later.

I wish to direct a couple of questions to the parliamentary assistant on a subject about which we have heard something in the past couple of days, namely, strawberries. If I had known that this item was coming up to-day I would have reserved until this occasion a part of the remarks I made yesterday. May I say that it has never been suggested by anyone in British Columbia at any time that the ceiling should be lifted from strawberries, because we know that that is impossible at this date. We did ask that the price be based on cost of production. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that it will be much more convenient to answer my questions to-day because it will not entail messages being sent up and down each moment in order to get a direction.
I wish to quote as an authority on this subject the minister himself. He stated that the reason for the ceiling was to prevent inflation. Now, we never suggested at any time in British Columbia that there should be an inflationary price. What We did urge Was that the ceiling should be based on cost of production and a reasonable profit for 1944. Last year for the first time in British Columbia the price was based on white labour and white production, and the price, according to the minister, was 33 cents. Let me repeat, the minister said that they were definitely setting the ceiling in order to prevent inflation. May I remark in passing that yesterday I said nothing that could be regarded as antagonistic to the officials of the board, though I must say that in my opinion they do not know the first thing about berries. They are human beings who are trying to do a good job in connection with something they know nothing about.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I know that the hon. member for Fraser Valley does not want to repeat what has been said before in discussions in the committee. Yesterday we had a discussion lasting nearly two hours in connection with strawberries and raspberries and

War Appropriation-Finance

this afternoon the question has come up again. I would ask hon. members to try as fax as possible to avoid repetition.

I do not want to repeat anything, Mr. Chairman, but I am quoting the highest authority in the house, the minister himself, who declared that the [DOT] prices were set with a view to preventing inflation. Let me read what he said as reported at page 3322 of Hansard of May 29:
In 1943 the average figure for Nova Scotia was 22 cents; New Brunswick, 19 cents; Quebec, 17 cents; Ontario, 18 cents; British Columbia, 33 cents.
Before I go on with my argument, may I say that on no account do I want prices reduced in other provinces. I do not know what their cost of production is. But the minister's statement is based on the figures he quoted, and if there has been an increase in all the other provinces and there has been no inflation, where is the inflation in British Columbia? Let us take the beautiful province of Nova Scotia, a province which is fortunately situated. In 1939 the price was 10 cents; in 1940, 11 cents; in 1941, 13 cents; and in 1942, 14 cents-the highest of any province of the dominion. Yet in 1944 Nova Scotia-and I do not say that the figure is too high-the price is set at 22 cents. My point is this: Why is it that British Columbia is the only province that is told it must come down? In every other province the price is higher than ever before, and that has not resulted in inflation; yet we are told that there is danger of inflation in British Columbia, where, as I say, we have the price based for the first time on the white man's production costs.	.
I am going to ask the officials of the wartime prices and trade board to take into consideration some of the facts which I am about to state. In British Columbia the minimum wages effective from a date before 1938, so far as the canneries are concerned were: at least 85 per cent of male employees, per hour, 38 cents; at least 90 per cent of women, 30 cents; not more than 15 per cent of male employees, 28 cents, and not more than 10 per cent of women employees, 25 cents.
I will not give New Brunswick, but let us take Ontario prices. In cities and towns with a population of from 5,000 to 30,000, the wages were 22 cents for women and 15 cents for girls under 18. Anyone who knows anything about the jam canneries knows that the average girl employee is under 18. As regards the rest of the province, in towns and villages with population from 2,000 to 5,000-and that is where the average farm cannery is situated -the wages for women was 20 cents and girls
[The Chairman.!
under eighteen, 15 cents. Compare that with a minimum of 30 cents in British Columbia. Can anyone contend that we have inflation in British Columbia?
The situation in Quebec is even worse. I did not think it was possible to have anything worse than I have already shown, but here are the figures for the province of Quebec, taking temporary employees-and the average employee in a cannery is a temporary employee. For men-mark this, men, regular employees-the figure is 25 cents; for women, 17 cents; and in the city of Montreal and outside Montreal the figures are, men, 20 cents and women, 15 cents. I thought that was bad enough; I did not think it was possible to have slave labour of this kind. However, we find that the average employee in Quebec canneries, between June 15 and October 15, received, men, 14 cents an hour, and women, 14 cents an hour.
I would ask the officials of the board to explain to me where the inflation comes in in British Columbia when every other province has had an increase this year as compared with last year and when we in British Columbia have to compete against such wages as I have quoted. I should like to know whether the cost of production is taken into consideration. When it requires 30 cents a quart to produce in Ontario, and when we find such disgraceful wages as 14 cents an hour being paid to men working in a cannery, how can we produce at 27 cents? I do not say that 30 cents is too high for Ontario and Quebec. I do not think the farmers are getting too much, but it is unreasonable to expect the farmers in British Columbia to swallow hook, line and sinker the nonsense that is put out by men who, as the member for York-Sunbury says, know nothing about berries and who evidently do not take these facts into consideration.
I defy the deputy or any official of the board to say that any farm organization or member of parliament was consulted in arriving at the figures. I admit that I am a little bit bitter about this, but I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there is nothing personal in my remarks, so far as the members of the board are concerned. Indeed, two gentlemen who have to do with jam come from British Columbia. I say, however, that the farmers of British Columbia, judging by the wires that I have received, are anxious to know, and they are entitled to know, how the figure was arrived at. I particularly wish the parliamentary assistant to tell me whether the cost of production was taken into consideration, when we are compelled to ship our berries, our processed fruit, where we are directed.

War Appropria lion-Finance
No doubt in war time that is necessary. How is it that the price in Ontario of 30 cents for fresh fruit is dropped to 19 cents?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Thirty cents.

The price of 30 cents in Ontario is dropped to 19 cents after June 24. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was challenged yesterday by the Minister of Finance, but he was correct; he knew what he was talking about. They want the cream at all times. Why the increase to 30 cents and then the drop to 19 cents? I should like the parliamentary assistant to explain why that is. I will prove my point by their own figures.
When the time comes for canning, Ontario must import processed berries from British Columbia. The manufacturer in British . Columbia can pay up to 12 cents per pound after that date, but of course he is not going to pay that for jam berries. For argument's sake say that he pays 10 cents a pound, but 12 cents is the maximum he is allowed to pay. He will offer 10 cents a pound and say, "Take it or leave it; I have to compete with the cheap labour and cheap manufacture in the east." We are compelled to ship our processed berries to eastern Canada. I am not quarrelling with that because at the present time we do not have the manufacturing facilities in British Columbia. It is a peculiar fact that when you follow that through you find that 30 cents is being paid in Ontario with its cheap labour, and then 19 cents when they want to manufacture. It should be noted that at December 31, 1943, there were 8,200,000 pounds of fruit pulp in British Columbia as against 3,800,000 pounds in 1942. I doubt if any of the great producers' organizations in British Columbia were consulted. I doubt if any hon. member from British Columbia was consulted in connection with this price ceiling for berries. I doubt very much if the jam manufacturers of British Columbia were not consulted before this figure was arrived at. I want the parliamentary assistant to explain to me how they arrived at this. Was the cost of production taken into consideration? Were the jam manufacturers consulted before the ceiling was set?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I thought we had our strawberry festival yesterday. I am afraid I am not very well prepared to deal with the questions my hon. friend has asked. As I recall, he asked how the price was arrived at. It was arrived at by the fruits and vegetable administration, of which his fellow British Columbian, Mr. Chambers, is the administrator. I am informed that it was arrived at after consultation with the officials of the department of agriculture of British Columbia
100-213i
and after Mr. Chambers had visited that province. That was so far as the price in that part of Canada is concerned.
Was the horticultural council called in?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot say.

May I ask a
question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I could cover the points raised by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The parliamentary
assistant should be allowed to give his answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I was just trying to cover the other question which was asked. The hon. member asked how the price was arrived at, and I pointed out that consultations had taken place before that price was fixed. As the minister said yesterday, the 1943 crop in British Columbia was about one-quarter of normal. Speaking from memory, it was some 2,500,000 quarts as against about 5,500,000 quarts for the year before and some 10,000,000 quarts for the preceding year. There was no price ceiling on berries last year, and to use a slang phrase, the berry growers in British Columbia went to town with their prices. I do not blame them, but the fact is that they got a very good price for their berries last year. There was no ceiling in effect and average price received in 1943 by the berry growers of British Columbia was 33 cents per quart as against 12 cents per quart the preceding year.
Do I understand you to say that the average price received for all berries was 33 cents?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am informed that the Dominion of Canada Department of Agriculture reports show that the average price received in 1943 by the growers in British Columbia was 33 cents a quart as against an average price of 12 cents a quart in 1942. In other words, it was better than two and a half times the price received in the preceding year, and, as the minister indicated yesterday, about four times the average price for the preceding four years.
I think the cost of production of agricultural products is probably one of the hardest things to determine, but it is a pretty fair indication as to whether a return is reasonable when the price set is double the prices received over an average period. It is true that the ceiling price fixed this year for British Columbia strawberries is about nine or ten cents below the 1943 prices, but, as I have indicated, those prices were more than double 'the 1942 prices. In the judgment of the board, and
War Appropriation-Finance

particularly of Mr. Chambers, who is the fruits and vegetable administrator, that was a fair price, both to the producer and to the consumer. I am afraid I cannot give any more information as to how the price was arrived at. If I had to make the decision I certainly would not have fixed a higher price.
Mr. CRUICKSHANIv: I should like to follow that question through. As I understand the parliamentary assistant he said that the average price received in British Columbia last year was 33 cents a quart.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
And he intimated that that is how they arrived at the figure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That was one factor that was taken into consideration in fixing what was thought to be a proper price this year. As I think the minister indicated yesterday British Columbia was the only province in which there was a roll-back of prices, to use the jargon of price control. It was thought that the prices last year in British Columbia had got so much out of line with prices in other parts of Canada that some roll-back was necessary.

I am afraid that that is just what I expected the board would use in arriving at their prices. I appreciate the fact that the parliamentary assistant is not a berry man, although I think he knows a great deal more-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not a question of berries; the same principle would apply to any other commodity.
I think he has a great deal more experience with berries than any of the people on the board at that time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have picked a lot in my time.

The parliamentary assistant tells me that 33 cents was the average price. That is not correct. Last year only approximately ten per cent of the berries were sold at 33 cents. That is according to the board's own figures.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am taking the figures of the Department of Agriculture; I have no personal knowledge of this matter.

I am speaking from personal knowledge and I defy the board to correct me in Hansard or anywhere else. Only approximately ten per cent of the berries were sold at that price. It is unfortunate that these officials over there do not know anything about growing or selling berries.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure that every hon. member of the committee heard the same questions asked and the same answers given yesterday. After almost four months of discussion in committee I do not think there should be so much repetition. I know that is the sense of the members.

When I am out of order I will appreciate being told.
The 'CHAIRMAN: It is not a question of being out of order. [DOT] Surely the committee has reached a stage in the proceedings where there should not be so many repetitions.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I ami repeating myself and I will have Hansard checked. The impression has been given to the committee that the berry farmers of British Columbia received an average of 33 cents a quart last year for their berries. That is absolutely incorrect, and I want to correct it. Only ten per cent were sold at that price. I shall quote some figures. In 1941 one factory at Haney shipped out 49,058 pounds of fruit in crates; last year, 1943, they shipped 7,017 pounds. Then they tell me that that is the average figure arrived at. Surely that cannot be the average figure arrived at. This is of vital importance, Mr. Chairman, to 3,000 berry farmers in the province of British Columbia. Now it is a question whether they keep their farms or not. This question could have been settled here in five minutes if the private members had been consulted before this order was brought down.
There is another thing about which I feel very keenly. It is not inflation to increase the price in Ontario and Quebec. Apparently Ontario and Quebec run Canada. Then in Nova Scotia, one particularly situated province where the price has been higher than in any other province in Canada, the price is increased-and that is not inflation! You can use your imagination.

When we began this discussion this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, we were on poultry, and we have since wandered to beef cattle, strawberries and the like. I was very much interested in what the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox had to say. I live not too far from him, and I know that in his county they have a real poultry show every1 year. I hardly understand how it was that these producers had to sell their poultry at the ungraded price. In our county for some years we have held a little poultry show; we have had a government grader come to the show to grade the poultry, and the poultry was all sold on that basis. If the producers mentioned had to sell their poultry ungraded, that was unfair. We have been educated for

IFar Approprialion-Finance
years .to grow high-grade products, not only poultry but apples and all kinds of farm products, and surely we should be able to sell our products on a graded basis. While it does not come under the wartime prices and trade board, steps should be taken to see that the poultry is graded because the producers should not be compelled to sell poultry ungraded.
I hold no brief for the wartime prices and trade board. I do not think any hon. member does. This board brings possibly as much grief as any board we ever had.
You can be assured of that.

But I believe in giving
credit where credit is due. The board has done some things well; it has done a real job. When I have brought individual cases to their attention they have always been courteous and willing to consider the situation, and when they see the situation as we see it we get pretty good results. On the other hand, a great many of these men on the wartime prices and trade board know very little about the thing they are trying to control. I do not suppose you could find on the board a man who had any experience in the production end of agriculture.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Grisdale.

While I appreciate the
fact that the officials of the board will go to the federation of agriculture or some other organization for information and advice, at the same time from some of the decisions they give one must conclude that they know very little about what they are trying to control. But as I said before, they should be given credit where credit is due, and they have done some real good work.
There is too much spread between the producer and the consumer so far as poultry is concerned. There is no reason why the farmer should sell at 33 cents and the retailer sell at from 45 to 47 cents. That is too much of a spread. If the board is going to control prices it should step in and set the price at what the consumer has to pay.
Were you ever consulted by the board about anything?

No, but I have always
been received courteously by the board, and any case that I have brought before them has received consideration.
And no action.
Yes, action.

Why is the price of fertilizer, especially orchard fertilizer, set at from one to two dollars higher in the maritime
provinces than in the province of Quebec? In Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island the price was set at $34 a ton, and in Quebec $32.50 a ton. In Ontario the price was set at $34.50 a ton. The laid-down cost of the raw material is the same in every province and at all stations because the government pays the freight on the raw material.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will try to get that
information.

Why is it that in the maritime provinces the wholesalers are said to be allowed a larger profit than in the other provinces? That was given to me as one of the reasons why the consumer paid a higher price in the maritime provinces than in any other province. I would like to know why these wholesalers were allowed a special profit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Is the hon. member referring to fertilizer?
Mr- HANSON (York-Sunbury): Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have a memorandum
here which I would like to look over before I give my hon. friend an answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee realizes that this subject has been lengthily discussed on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and I believe that the answer which the parliamentary assistant may now be going to read is to be found in Hansard of a few weeks ago.
We had better hear his answer.

speechtext: With reference to the question asked by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton and the supplementary question asked by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the point which the hon. member for York-Sunbury made probably has something to do with it. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the price of fertilizer during the basic period or to-day. I will try to get a little more
War Appropriation-Finance

information on the subject. I have a memorandum here which indicates, as was suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that the differential was based on the difference in discounts in the basic period.
So far as discounts go, the volume is much heavier in the maritime provinces than in Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

I will get the information
