speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to make
a few general remarks in connection with the wartime prices and trade board. What I say will be critical but I trust that the parliamentary assistant and his officials will accept my suggestions as intended to be constructive.
I think we all must agree, despite the many criticisms we may make about the work and the administration of this board, that its job has been a very necessary and very important one in this time of war. As previous speakers have pointed out, difficulties have arisen largely because of the way in which the policies of the board have been administered. I feel that in particular the fault has been the failure of the board to win the confidence of the Canadian people, and I offer that criticism in the hope that the board might consider taking steps even at this late date to try to overcome that deficiency by winning the confidence of our people.
One thing that strikes me and a great many other people is the fact that apparently the government and its boards are always right. It does not matter what question is asked or what complaint is made; the government, or a board as in this case, always has an answer which is supposed to set aside the complaint. It seems to me that one means of gaining the confidence of the Canadian people in the activities of this board would be for the board to admit that this is a terrific problem which they have undertaken, that the board is faced with difficulties, and that it needs the help and the understanding of the people.
Let me quote one or two examples. Until last fall, one of a number of restrictions which the wartime prices and trade board had imposed was that very silly one against two pairs of trousers with a man's suit and also prohibiting cuffs on a man's trousers; and as hon. members on the Liberal side of the house will recall, suddenly, following a meeting of the National Liberal Federation in Ottawa last fall, that order was changed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Pure coincidence.
Mr. KNOWLES. "Pure coincidence", of course. Similarly with the other relaxations which were effected at that time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What were those?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Such as rubber. I know that Liberal members of the house rather set aside what the parliamentary assistant has said, by claiming credit for what was done-

Surely,
they have, all over the country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-because of the fuss they raised on that occasion. I suggest that that kind of thing does not build up confidence on the part of the people in the board's decisions.
Another matter is that of deterioration in the quality of goods. During the course of this war, as the cost of living has gone up- though admittedly kept in control by the board as compared with what happened during the last war-one of the things which people in general and housewives in particular have tried to point out is that there was a deterioration in quality. We have raised the matter on the floor of this chamber, and last year and the year before the Minister of Finance, of course, always had an answer-there had not been any deterioration in quality which the wartime prices and trade board had not taken into consideration. Well, the parliamentary assistant can make the statement again to-day, but the housewives of the country find it difficult to believe; and I am simply suggesting that if, in the propaganda the board puts out, in the radio talks, in its general appeals to the public, it would go so far as to admit that some of these unfortunate things have occurred, perhaps it would win some of the confidence which is so necessary for it in its difficult job.
The same is true in connection with the increase in the cost of living, another point which has been raised here a number of times. Material is always produced to prove that it has not risen any higher than the indices show, despite what the housewife and the average citizen may know. It does not seem to me that it is ever to the disadvantage of a government to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Not only is that true with respect to the matters which I have mentioned but also with respect to the supply of goods available. From time to time hon. members representing different sections of the community have mentioned the shortage of clothing for people in the farming communities, or the shortage of baby clothing, and so on, and the minister or his parliamentary assistant always had an answer; the government is always quite efficient and always doing a perfect job.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Oh, no; we never laid claims to perfection-never.

War Appropriation-Finance
You never admitted an error.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes; I have admitted errors on occasions too.
Never.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We certainly never laid claims to perfection.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Are these imported or
domestically produced?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They are imported, but are made available in this country, and people are allowed to go ahead and purchase such luxury goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is a big tax on them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
People generally have the notion that the job of the wartime prices and trade board and the aim of government policy in general are to avoid the spending of money on luxury goods, so as to get down to the real business on hand. It seems to me that this sort of thing should be avoided if at all possible, and that when it is not, it works against the success of the job which the wartime prices and trade board is trying to do. This advertisement appeared, I might say, at a time when the victory loan drive was being launched. I saw it myself in Winnipeg papers which I receive every day, and it also came to me from several correspondents in Winnipeg who were quite incensed when they saw this advertisement in the papers.
I offer this suggestion in a critical vein; at the same time I do it in what I hope is a constructive manner, because I feel there is yet a long pull ahead as regards the price
control policy of the government, and if the board is to do its work effectively, in the light of the criticisms which the parliamentary assistant is getting from all over the chamber to-day-most heatedly from his own side-it must take every step to win the confidence of the people, and I trust that the parliamentary assistant will take seriously and pass on to his officials the suggestions which I have made.
Mr. JOHNSTON (Bow River)1: I should like to make a small correction of the statement I made a few moments ago to the parliamentary assistant as regards bank charges for accounts established in respect of coupons. I stated that I had received a letter from the department. That is not so; I got letters from some of my constituents in this regard, and I was intending to write to the minister's department, but I recalled that the question had been asked at a previous time. I therefore telephoned the returns officer, and together we found in Hansard where this question was asked. I should like to read the answer; for all practical purposes it was the same as I indicated to the minister a while ago. The report is to be found on page 1990, March 30, 1944. It is in answer to the hon. member for Eglinton, who asked, with reference to gasoline coupon rationing, what service the banks render and what remuneration would be received. It is stated:
The basis of payment is as follows: 25 cents per account opened; 6 cents per debit or credit entry; 12 cents per 1,000 coupons handled. The basis of these charges is subject to review following an analysis to be made within a few months after gasoline rationing coupon banking becomes effective.
I would suggest, while we are on this subject, that this is a very substantial return for the banking service rendered. I was amazed when I looked up the answer to this question and found how exceedingly generous was the remuneration for this service. I think the committee will be really interested to know, when the parliamentary assistant brings down his final statement, the amount of money that is to be paid to the banks for this service. It seems to me it will be tremendous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I said a moment ago I am going to get the information and give the hon. member a detailed answer on the coupon bank.
I think the parliamentary assistant to the minister will admit that the object of the wartime prices and trade board was to control prices?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
And to assure adequate
civilian supplies. It has a double function, remember.
War Appropriation-Finance

If it failed to control prices then it did not accomplish the object for which it was set up. Let us take the years 1928-29 and compare them with the present day. I think that would be a fair comparison. We had no wartime prices and trade board in 1928-29, and! yet we find in those years that the price of cattle was higher and the price of beef lower than it is at the present time. I cannot give the figures but I could get them from the statistics. But the price of cattle this year is lower and the price of beef higher than it was in 1928-29.

Because
there is a ceiling.

I do not wish to cover any of the ground that has been already covered, but I wish to add to what the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox said in regard to the price of poultry. Does the department take into consideration the grade? If that is not taken into consideration the grade can be stepped up at any time with a resulting loss to the farmer. I want to be clear on that point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Does the hon. member want an answer to that now?
Yes.	.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is a most elaborate scale of prices for poultry, depending upon the grades, starting with special, grade A, grade B, and so forth. It varies with the different parts of the country. It is all contained as a schedule to administrative order A-893. The schedule of ceiling prices covers a full page and fixes special ceiling prices for different grades of poultry such as special grade, milk-fed; grade A, milk-fed; grade B, milk-fed; special grade A; grade B; grade C, and so on, with different ceilings for each recognized grade as defined by the Department of Agriculture.
Does the inspector see that the grade goes to the consumer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That poultry is inspected
and graded, of course, by an inspector of the Department of Agriculture. The wartime prices and trade board has nothing to do with that. On the point raised by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox that it was not possible to get the poultry graded in the town of Napanee early in December because there were no inspectors there, I take it he would agree with me that if the poultry raisers had wished to do so they could1 have shipped the poultry to the packing plants and had them graded there and received the price for the grading. That is my advice.
They could not bring them back to the show, though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not know whether they could show them or not, but they could ship them and get the graded price.

According to the statement of the parliamentary assistant to the minister, his department has nothing to do with seeing that the established grade is enforced; that is, if turkeys are sold, the men who get them cannot sell them as grade A if they were graded as B's?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The grading of poultry is clearly the function of the Department of Agriculture, and their inspectors establish the grade. If the poultry has been classified as grade A and the dealer attempts to sell them as special grade A, if our enforcement officers can catch him they would prosecute him. The wartime prices and trade board is charged with the responsibility of enforcing the ceiling. The ceilings are based on the grade of the particular bird that is being sold. If a dealer has purchased grade B and fraudulently attempts to sell it as grade A, the wartime prices and trade board would endeavour through its inspectors to catch him, and if he is caught they will prosecute him.
There is no law or order set up to make sure that the farmer's grade goes through to the consumer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He is entitled to get the price which is fixed for the grade of poultry that he is selling. If he sells to a wholesaler and his poultry is graded grade A, he is entitled to get grade A wholesale prices.

I understand that, but there is no protection from the farmer to the consumer to ensure that the middleman cannot raise a B to an A. Your department does not do anything about it, to see that a man does not get away with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a very serious offence. It applies to any commodity that is subject to grading. I do not know what my hon. friend means by "protection". The law is there. If it is broken and the offender is caught, he is prosecuted. That is the only answer I can give. It is a serious offence to alter the grades of poultry or any other agricultural product which is graded in accordance with the requirements of the Department of Agriculture.

My point is that it is as essential to see that the grades are maintained as that the price is maintained. When you alter the grades you alter the price. As far as ungraded poultry is concerned, progressive farmers think that field is the happy hunting-ground for private enterprise.

War Appropriation-Finance
I do not wish to cover the ground gone over by the hon. member for Souris, but I should like to add a little to what he said. Under the regulations to-day the farmer is deducted $3.50 for one pound overweight of pork. Those regulations have been set up by the wartime prices and trade board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should like to say that the wartime prices and trade board covers a very wide field, but it has nothing to do with the grading of pork products. I would suggest that my hon. friend direct his inquiries and criticisms to the Minister of Agriculture when he is here, because certainly I, personally, am not competent to deal with questions involving the grading of pork. The wartime prices and trade board has no control whatsoever over them.
Perhaps I am all mixed up here. The wartime prices and trade board appointed the meat board,

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; the Department of Agriculture set up the meat board.
No; it comes under the wartime prices and trade board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; it has nothing to do with the board. We have enough headaches of our own.
Donald Gordon was the man who dominated things in the meat board in Manitoba, and if he is in the wartime prices and trade board he is not in the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that the meat board-
If the parliamentary assistant says that his department has nothing to do with it I have to take it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised, and I know it to be a fact, that the Canadian meat board was created and set up last June under the Department of Agriculture by order in council. There is nothing in this appropriation which has anything to do with the Canadian meat board.

I put a question on the order paper about a man by the name of J. K. Smith, truck controller in the province of Quebec. I received an answer from the parliamentary assistant to the minister on May 22, 1944. My questions were as follows:
1.	Is Mr. J. K. Smith, truck controller for the province of Quebec, an employee of the dominion government or a dollar a year man?
The answer is:
An employee of the dominion government, wartime prices and trade board.
2.	In either case, since when?
The answer is:
May 1, 1942.
3.	What was his previous occupation?
The answer is:
From 1900 to 1920, Mr. Smith was engaged in various phases of freight traffic handling, becoming in 1918 assistant to the general traffic manager of the freight tariff bureau ot the Canadian Rational Railways. In 1920 he joined the Acadia Sugar Refining Company, Montreal, as traffic manager, and in 1922 was appointed manager of the transportation bureau, M.ontieal board of trade, from which organization he is presently on loan to this board.
4.	Will a bilingual employee be appointed in his stead?
The answer is:
No appointment is necessary as the position is now filled.
The majority of the people of the city of Montreal speak the French language. This parliament passed a law-I do not remember the year, but the measure was sponsored by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmoreney- under which the government is obliged, in making appointments to governmental organizations, to appoint men who speak the language of the majority of those living in the locality. Mr. Smith does not speak one word of French. If he can speak it he does not want to do so. When he is mad at something; when he differs with a visitor over a matter of policy, be it fascism or anything else, he asks for the police and wants the visitor thrown out. The hon. gentleman must be aware of that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, I am not, but I will look into it.

That is what he did with Mr. Fillion, secretary of the Catholic union of farmers in Quebec. The question went on:
5. If not, why not?
The answer is:
Mr. Smith's services are quite satisfactory and he has several French-speaking assistants.
Well, his services are not satisfactory. The government is obliged to appoint a man speaking the language of the majority of the people in the locality, and Mr. Smith does not speak French. Why do we have to fight all the time for details? We are not tired of fighting, but we do not like it. The government should take care of that situation; it should pay heed when representations are made by serious people in regard to employees who are not able to speak both languages, especially in the province of Quebec. Imagine a government employee in Toronto or Winnipeg speaking French and not a word of English, able to give satisfactory service because he had English-speaking assistants!
War Appropriation-Finance

He would not last very long. Why should we be expected to put up with this sort of thing in Quebec? I know the hon. gentleman speaks French, so that I should like to read an article which appeared in Le Droit of Tuesday May 23.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Le Devori?

No; Le Droit. It would not be too bad if it had been Le Devoir, because that newspaper represents a good portion of the opinion of Quebec.
(Translation): Such a thing'would not happen in Ontario.
Some time ago, a French-language agricultural weekly, Le Terre de chest nous, upbraided Mr. J. K. Smith, director trucking in the province of Quebec under the dominion government. It charged that official, among other things, with inefficiency in the performance of his duties, because of his ignorance of the language spoken by four-fifths of the people m the province of Quebec.
The matter had an echo in the house-
That relates to my question.
Here is the reply made by the government on Monday. Mr. J. Iv. Smith has been employed by the Canadian government on the staff of the 1942^mf3 ^r*ees an<^ trade board since May 1,
The reply I have quoted a few moments ago is then given. The article goes on:
Of course, such a thing would not happen in Ontario. It would never occur even to the dominion government to appoint a director of trucking who could only speak French, and if against all possibility, that was done and should the government, in reply to a question asked by a member in that connection, state that the said director had assistants who spoke English the representatives of the Ontario people in Ottawa would surely not accept such an explanation. An uproar would be raised against the action of the government and the latter would hasten to rectify their blunder.
(Text):
So that I ask the parliamentary assistant if this situation will be cleared up, if Mr. Smith will be replaced. It is only fair to the people of Quebec, to the farmers of that province, that we have in Montreal a chief speaking both languages, or at least the language of the majority. French is official, as well as English, and we hope the government will listen to our representations. I trust the parliamentary assistant will look into the matter seriously, because we will come back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I know Mr. Smith slightly, but I do not know whether his knowledge of French is good or bad. I was under the impression that he spoke both languages.
Well, then, he does not want to speak French.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As to that I cannot say. Mr. Smith has had a long experience in the 
transportation business, as was indicated in the answer to the question asked by my hon. friend.
I do not deny that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Smith knows the work thoroughly, and I am advised that he has several French-speaking assistants. My hon. friend will realize that these special war jobs are not permanent positions in the civil service, to which men are appointed for a period of years. Many of these positions are filled by men who are on loan because of their special technical qualifications, and I believe that is the case with Mr. Smith. Because of his special knowledge of transportation problems he was appointed transport controller, or whatever it is, in the province of Quebec. I have no knowledge of the instances mentioned by my hon. friend of alleged discourtesy on the part of Mr. Smith toward people who came to see him, but most certainly I will make inquiries and see what there is in that particular charge. I have here a letter which was written by L'Association du Transport Interurbain Inc. of Montreal, signed by the secretary, Mr. Archambault, and addressed to the chairman of the board, with reference to Mr. Smith, and I should like to read it to the committee to indicate how his services are viewed by one association in Montreal, at any rate. The letter is as follows:
Mr. Donald Gordon,
Chairman,
Wartime Prices and Trade Board, 490 Sussex street,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir:
Our association has learned with the greatest surprise that certain representations have been made regarding the present controller of transport at Montreal, Mr. J. K. Smith.
Our association feels that Mr. J. K. Smith has been doing his utmost to uphold the interest of the public in general and to carry out the regulations that have been imposed by the prices and trade board in order to control the business of transportation iby truck and assist in the conservation of gasoline and tires.
It is obvious, in our opinion, that certain individuals feel that the present restrictions impose a hardship upon them and that the controller of transport should be the person to blame.
It has been resolved by the directors of our association to forward you an expression of their opinion to the effect that Mr. J. K. Smith has been serving the best interests of the public and that they do not recommend any change in .this appointment.
Yours most truly,
Association du Transport Interurbain Inc.
per C. Archambault,
Secretary.
The letter is dated May 20, 1944. As my hon. friend knows, I am just as anxious as

War Appropriation-Finance
anyone in this house or this country to have both languages spoken, and my hon. friend knows that my own facility in his native tongue is reasonably good.
I really deprecate that, in the case of a man who is doing a war job such as Mr. Smith is doing, and doing it well, according to my information, putting it on the basis that because he is operating in the province of Quebec, where admittedly the majority of the people speak French, that being their mother tongue, he must also speak French. I am not satisfied that he has not some knowledge of French, although I daresay, like a good many English-speaking Canadians in the province of Quebec, his knowledge of that language is not as good as it should be. Nevertheless, I venture to say that he understands French and probably understands it pretty well. He may not be able to converse in the language as fluently as he would like, but I have no doubt that he does understand it. That is about all I have to say. As regards the direct question which my hon. friend has put, as to whether Mr. Smith will be replaced or not, my answer at the moment is no.

I do not deny the ability of Mr. Smith, and I hope the parliamentary assistant does not deny that an official of any department should be obliged to speak the language of the majority of the people in the locality.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I should point out that, according to my understanding, this is not a civil service appointment. Mr. Smith was appointed, as many were appointed to these war jobs, by order in council and not on the recommendation of the civil service commission.
Then the parliamentary assistant says that Mr. Smith, not being a civil employee, is not compelled to speak French?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall have to verify this. I understand that this is not a civil service appointment.

If Mr. Smith understands French he should not get mad when anyone speaks French to him. He does not have to throw people out, and that is what he did. He called for the police. I do not deny his ability, but I deny his courtesy toward people who have dealings with the farmers. All the farmers in Quebec do not speak English, though a great many of them do. I repeat, no member of this house from the Englishspeaking provinces would stand for such a situation, and they would be right. Why should we have to stand for it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I promised my hon. friend that I would look into the statements he has made as to Mr. Smith's attitude toward people who came to see him. I have no knowledge of that myself.
I hope my hon. friend will look into it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I take it that my hon. friend is giving this on hearsay; he was not present at the interview.

I was not present but I have letters that prove it is true. Mr. Fillion of "Terre de Chez Nous" wrote himself that he had to go out of Mr. Smith's office, and we can believe Mr. Fillion as well as anyone else.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am not questioning Mr. Fillion's word. I am saying that I shall have the matter looked into.
Mr. 'GAUTHIER: It is not hearsay on my part.

The matter I am about to discuss should perhaps be brought up under a subsequent item, but seeing that we have wandered all over the place, perhaps it will not be objected to if I attempt to discuss it at this moment. I do not suppose there has been a session in the last forty years when at some time or another the question of sugar has not been considered in its many ramifications. One of the things that strikes me as peculiar, looking back over the records, is that the speeches as reported in Hansard ten and fifteen years ago on this question resemble the speeches of the last few years. This subject was debated at some length during the last session and it has been brought up once or twice again this year. During the years from 1930 to 1935 the question of sugar, in its relation to the sugar-beet industry particularly, was debated at considerable length and a special subcommittee was appointed in that period, from the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, to make a study into the sugar-beet industry and to report to the government of the day. An exhaustive study of the subject was made at that time. The records show that it was conducted here over many weeks and many witnesses were brought here, growers as well as refiners. After a thorough study of the subject they submitted to the house a report from which I will read a portion of the final analysis that was presented:
Your committee therefore recommends that in view of the existing tariff on sugar and in consideration of the substantial payments being made to agriculture and labour by the ibeet sugar factories at present in operation, the cane sugar refineries should undertake to provide for
33S4
War Appropriation-Finance

a gradual increase in factory facilities for the refining of beet sugar in Canada, and that, with the additional advantages in freight rates to points in the middle west, heretofore described, factory facilities should now be steadily increased in western areas where beets are grown, and thereby make it possible to produce from beets a more substantial percentage of the sugar consumption of Canada.
On March 20, when the subject was discussed in the house, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) read that statement into the record. The hon. member is no doubt a loyal party follower and it rather amused me to read this statement he made in connection with it:
I Tead from that report to show that the government of that day and the agriculture committee of that day were ready to encourage the production of ibeet sugar in Canada. Since that time there has been a considerable increase in the production of beet sugar in Manitoba. There is a splendid refinery located there and I suggest to all hon. members that they visit it. It is one of the best in Canada and it has great possibilities. I say these few words to show that the party of that day was interested in increasing the beet sugar industry of Canada.
There is no doubt that the majority of the members of the committee were taken from the government in power. That was the normal thing to do. But actions speak louder than words and there was no evidence that the party in power was favourable to the production of beet sugar, because nothing was ever done by the federal government to encourage that industry. At that time a delegation came from Lambton to interview the Prime Minister of the day because they could visualize another refinery or two in that part of the country. They had an interview with the Prime Minister of that day and he was quite conversant with the sugar-beet industry. They said that he talked intelligently on the subject, but he gave them the old stock in trade, which is given by a great many people: "You may rest assured that we shall go over this matter very carefully and give it every consideration."
At. that time the beet-sugar industry was at a very low ebb. The price of sugar was very low, and naturally the contract price of beets would be based on the wholesale price of sugar. There were many reasons for that. During the war of 1914-18 sugar production in the cane districts increased tremendously to take care of the sugar demands of the world. The beet industry in Europe at that time was very much disrupted and was out of production. After the war the sugar-beet industry came back into production and the cane industry kept up production with the result that there soon developed a world surplus of sugar. This became quite acute 
and in 1922-23 sugar became so cheap that it could be purchased in some of the cane sugar countries at as low as fifty-five cents a hundred pounds. That was a very low price and it was almost impossible to compete against it. In 1936 the retail price of sugar in our western districts was $4.80 a hundred or $3.80 a hundred without the excise tax. A conference was called to consider the world supply of sugar and, as was mentioned the other night in the house, this was held in London from April 5 to July 6. Twenty-two countries were summoned to the conference, and I have the report before me. I should' like to read an item or two from the report as follows:
The summoning of the international sugar conference was the direct outcome of efforts which originated in the world of the world nionetary and economic conference which met in London in June-July, 1933. The economic commission of that conference devoted special and detailed attention to the problem of securing better coordination in the production and marketing of staple foodstuffs and raw materials and the application of the principle to individual commodities-one of which was sugar-was considered by special 'subcommittees appointed for the purpose.
Most of the countries represented were either producers or large consumers of sugar. Canada was not particularly interested in the production of sugar or in the curtailment of production to keep in line with world demand, so that the Canadian representative did not sign the agreement that was arrived at. I quote from the report:
Mr. Massey stated that after a necessarily hasty examination of the convention, the Canadian government regretted that it had not found it possible to authorize signature at present. Canada was, of course, sympathetic with the conference's desire to avert uneconomic production but her position at the conference as an importer and consumer of sugar was so different from that of almost all other countries, that the^ Canadian government desired a further period of time to study the effect of the specific proposals of the convention on that position, and in the light of that study to decide whether it would be possible to accede later.
The votes allocated to Canada were given to the United Kingdom and the United States. The amount of sugar produced by Canada at that time was a mere bagatelle when compared with the world's needs. Prior to that time Canada had with Great Britain, a treaty known as the British West Indies treaty which took care of the sugar supply of Canada. That treaty was revamped and reshaped in 1925 or 1926. Under the terms of the treaty sugar from the British West Indies was given $1. per 100 pounds preference over all other sugar imported into Canada, with the result that practically all the sugar we imported came from the British West Indies. This treaty

War Appropriation-Finance
was a perennial treaty in that it could be terminated only by either country giving twelve months notice of termination. It was suggested by the Canadian officials that the treaty was out of date, that Canada was not getting equal value by the terms of the treaty, and the result was that in 1938 Canada gave notice that she wished to terminate the treaty and that a new arrangement should be arrived at.
At that time the then Minister of Finance referred the question to the tariff board for inquiry and report. Hearings were held in Ottawa during the summer of 1938. During those hearings reference was made to the possibilities of the sugar beet industry. The board was headed by the late Mr. Justice Sedgewick, and hearings were held in the justice building. Before the report could be submitted war was declared and nothing further was done.	.
After the declaration of war in 1939 Great Britain took over all British empire supplies of sugar and appointed a sugar controller by the name of Sir William Rook. Shortly after that time Canada appointed Mr. S. R. Noble as sugar controller. I do not know how he came to be appointed, but I do know that he had considerable experience in Cuba in connection with the sugar industry. The point I want to make is that up to that time there had been no encouragement given to the sugar beet industry by any federal government in peace time.
Nevertheless the sugar, beet industry did develop. One of the first refineries in Canada was established at Wallaceburg in 1903 with the help of a provincial subsidy. About three years ago a refinery was established in Winnipeg also with the help of provincial support or subsidy. In 1944 a refinery will go into production in Quebec which also has the support of the provincial government. In spite of all handicaps the number of sugar-beet refineries in Canada has grown and to-day there are six modern refineries.
There are two refineries in Ontario which have a processing capacity of 45,000 acres and a total aggregate sugar producing capacity at normal yield of around 110,000,000 pounds. The two refineries in Alberta have a capacity of 35,000 acres, and would have a normal yield of around 110,000,000 pounds. The tonnage is a little higher in Alberta and the sugar content is a little higher. The refinery in Manitoba has a processing capacity of 20,000 acres with a sugar capacity of around 32,000,000 pounds. The refinery in Quebec, which will come into production this year, has a processing capacity of around 20,000 acres with a total production of 35,000,000 pounds.
If we had our total possible maximum production of sugar this year, from 120,000 acres, it would total around 287,000,000 or 290,000,000 pounds. The normal requirements of Canada are around 1,100,000,000 pounds, so that we would still require about 813,000,000 pounds to be imported to meet our needs. In a normal year that would be about one-quarter of our total requirements, but under our rationing system it would be approximately one-third of our requirements.
Since the United States entered the war Canada and that country have cooperated in connection with the supply of sugar. At the moment our principal supply is from Cuban sources. During the last war our main sources of supply were Sumatra, Java, Malaya, the Dutch Indies, and the Philippines, all of which are now under Japanese control. According to the authority of Sir William Rook, the world reserve of sugar is gradually' fading away. In 1942 this reserve was 3,000,000 tons; in 1943 it was 2,000,000 tons; in 1944 it was
1,000,000 tons, and it is expected that in 1945 our reserve of sugar will be practically used up. In other words, we shall be starting from scratch.	_	.
I have a press release which was issued on April 20 by the wartime prices and trade board, which reads:
Warning that world supplies of sugar are so short that larger rations may not be expected for the first year or two after the war was given recently by Sir William _ Rook, British sugar controller, during discussions with wartime prices and trade board officers.
Not only is there no surplus of sugar in the world to-day but the present supply is insufficient to meet even essential needs without strictly rationing, Sir William said. He termed "incomplete and inaccurate" the view that all that is lacking is enough shipping space to transport sugar from producing to consuming countries.
In Ontario to-day we have a pretty fair contract for the sugar-beet growers, especially when compared with other days. During the depression days the price was around $4.50 to $5 per ton, and a fair price would be a minimum of 19 per ton. On a sixteen per cent beet it would be Sll a ton, and on eighteen per cent beet $12.20 a ton. Labour costs are very high in Ontario and in all beet producing districts. The cost of hand labour for thinning, hoeing and harvesting would be $30 per acre; seed $2.25 per acre; fertilizer $3 per acre; delivery $12.25 per acre, making a total of $47.50.
Has the hon. member the additional cost in Alberta for the delivery of irrigation water?

I shall have that a little later. If we have an average
War Appropriation-Finance

crop of ten tons of beets to the acre in Ontario, and that has been a fair average over the years, at $9 a ton the gross return would be $90 per acre, from which deduct total costs of $47.50 and you have a net profit of $43.50 per acre, which should be the profit in a normal year. That does not include the farmer's own work, the cost of the land or anything he may do in connection with cultivating the land, so that the profit would not be very high.

How is the Ontario
farmer able to compete with the Alberta farmer whose beets have an eighteen per cent sugar content?
The sugar content in Ontario last year was eighteen per cent. There is not a great deal of difference in that respect. -
I understood the hon. member to say twelve per cent sugar content in Ontario.

Ten tons to the acre of eighteen per cent beets at S12.20 per ton would give a good gross yield. That includes subsidies. The Ontario government this year provided a subsidy of $1.55 a ton to the beet growers, and the beet growers appreciate that. The Ontario minister of agriculture, when presenting his bill to the house last winter, announced, according to press reports, that the government felt obliged to assist the beet industry in Ontario because the federal government would do nothing. That statement is hardly correct. It would have been correct for him to say that the federal government refused to give any more assistance to the beet industry at this time because they have already given two subsidies in the last two years. The first subsidy of half a cent a pound was given in 1942 on the price of refined sugar, and most of that subsidy went to the producer, though not all. There is a straight half a cent a pound subsidy because there was a stabilization fund built up after the outbreak of the war which the stabilization corporation has in what they call their inner reserve. Like the banks' inner reserves, we do not know what that reserve is, but they have this inner reserve. The second subsidy of half a cent a pound was given on February 1, 1944. This all went to the producer. A ton of beets that would have a test of eighteen per cent sugar content would run close to 300 pounds of sugar to the ton. That would mean close to $3 a ton subsidy from the federal government. The federal subsidies apply to all beets produced in Canada. Alberta probably gets a little better 
price for her sugar, but they have added freight rates and higher sugar prices; and after all the contract price of beets is based on the selling price of sugar. Sugar is selling in the retail stores to-day at eight cents a pound, which with one cent off for excise tax would make it seven cents.
The outlook for the Ontario crop is not too good, for many reasons. Labour is quite a problem. The crop must compete for labour with other crops in the district, such as corn, tobacco, beans, tomatoes. Mechanized equipment can be used for many of these other crops, whereas a lot of the work of growing beets must be done by hand. Ontario has a total capacity of 45,000 acres for growing beets. But I do not think we shall have more than 15,000 to 18,000 acres in beets in Ontario this year.
We have two refineries in Ontario, one in WallacebuEg and one in Chatham, both of which should operate at full capacity.
It is a mistaken idea that if we produce
290,000,000 pounds of sugar in Canada we shall have all the sugar we need, because all this sugar must go into the pool and be allocated by rationing. It is estimated that the Cuban yield will be 5 million long tons. If we produce our maximum amount of sugar and the United States produce their maximum amount of sugar, we probably could have our sugar ration increased.
What is the United States maximum ?

Last year the United States had thirty-two beet refineries which never operated at all. This year they are trying to get them all into production. I am not sure how they are getting along. One of the things we tried to do to increase our sugar-beet production this year was to suggest to the wartime prices and trade board-I am going to find fault with the board in this matter because it seems the proper thing to do-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is fashionable at any rate.

I feel that I should find fault with the board because the United States in order to increase its beet sugar production offered ration-free sugar to producers of beets. Anyone who produced one acre or more of sugar beets would get a free ration of sugar of twenty-five pounds per person. We made the suggestion to the wartime prices and trade board that a similar scheme should be adopted in Canada. The sugar controller was of the opinion that it would help.

War Appropriation-Finance
What does the hon. member mean by twenty-five pounds per person? Does he mean twenty-five pounds per person on the farm?

On the farm. Each extra acre of beets would produce around forty hundredweight of sugar, and if there were four people in the family, that would mean four twenty-five pound lots of free-ration sugar for them. They would put forty extra hundredweight into the pool and take one hundredweight out. That would mean that there would be thirty-nine extra hundredweight in the sugar pool.
The chairman of the board said that that would be discriminatory.	He asked, why
should people in fruit districts in Niagara, for instance, not get as much sugar as the people who produced sugar beets in Kent, Lambton or Essex? It would be discriminatory in the narrow sense, but if you produced a good many more acres of sugar beets you would be producing a lot more sugar, and in the long ran it would not be discriminatory. In the long ran we would have a greater supply of sugar.	We could have
adopted that policy which they are following in the United States. It is too late to do it this year. It would not probably have affected large operators, but it would have induced a great many small farmers who are not in the sugar beet business to produce one or two acres in order to get the free-ration sugar. Each extra acre would put forty hundredweight into the pool and probably take one hundredweight out. I am anxious to see how it works out in the United States.
There is one other thing I would mention in closing. If we want to get the industry back on a sound basis and want the beet growers to have confidence in the refiners, the Department of Agriculture should provide inspectors to go through the plants when the processing season is on for three or four months in the fall of the year and test the beets so as to assure the growers that they are getting a proper test of sugar content. The question is raised, of course, that that may be true of cream and what-not, but the fact remains that cream producers have a choice of where they are going to. send their product; the beet grower has none. I am quite sure that the refiners themselves would agree to that. It is the old story; people feel rightly or wrongly that the testing is all done by the refiners; there is no other way of shipping their beets; they must take it, whereas if the government had an inspector there to test those beets as they were processed and assure the growers
that they were getting full value, it would do much to restore confidence on the part of the growers.
I believe that we can grow sugar to-day in Canada successfully and economically. The refinery in Wallaceburg has operated successfully since 1903. The only year that it did not operate was 1942, owing to the lack of sufficient beets. Costs of production can be greatly reduced, with the new system of planting, with new split seed, by which they avoid the clusters. They are doing away with all the back-breaking labour; in Idaho they have a mechanized outfit which will pull beets, top them and load them in one operation. If that is developed in this country, I believe the government would be well advised to hang on to the beet industry, because it will play an important part in the post-war world and will absorb some of the labour which is bound to be a problem in the years of reconstruction. I call on the government to give the industry every assistance. Here are the figures covering the two refineries in Ontario for the 1940 crop only:
To beet growers-cash paid for crop	 $2,590,986
Supplies-coal, lime, bags, etc. ..	659,261
Freight to railways	 380,332
Labour-Factory and office payroll	 655,746
Total	 $4,286,325
The industry, I feel, is one which the government would be well advised to keep in operation and give all the support it possibly can.

Before the committee takes recess I wish to ask one question with respect to the sugar stabilization fund. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant has not the information, but this is what I want to know. It will be recalled that in the earlier stages of the war the sugar controller bought all the stocks in hand from the refineries and sold them back at an advance of half a cent a pound. The result was that several million dollars were collected; I had the figure once, but I am not sure what it is; perhaps the parliamentary assistant will let us know. I wish to be informed as to the purpose of establishing that fund at that time; has the same practice been consistently followed out to the present time; how much, if anything, has been disbursed in the interim; and how much remains? 1 should like to have a break-down of the disbursements; because, after all, the price of sugar was raised to the consumer to take care of that special fund; it did not come from the government
War Appropriation-Finance

or out of taxation; it was taken from the consuming public, who paid it in every purchase that it made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let that question stand I*will get the information.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I wish to bring before this committee a matter which comes under the heading of "administration", for which there is an appropriation of
815,600,000.	Under this heading the board makes expenditures of $156,600,000. Then there are additional subsidies of over $70,000,000 for food products in the Department of Agriculture, The board deals with the cost of living down to empty beer bottles and I am expected to discuss beer bottles although I am not an authority on this article.
The liquor business is the biggest business in which the government of Nova Scotia deals. Last year total sales amounted to $15,324,147.68. In this sum is the enormous outlay of $7,699,497.85 for beer. . It is estimated that the containers for this beer are estimated to be worth at least $1,000,000. The profits in handling the empties would be from $50,000 to $100,000 a year for the entire province. The wartime prices and trade board issued an order, No. A 236, in June, 1942, regulating the handling of liquor, wine and distillers' bottles, with no special reference to ale or beer bottles. This was a general order, I understand, applicable to the whole of Canada. It was cancelled soon after, since the supply of such bottles was sufficient to meet the needs of those requiring them.
On December 7, 1942, the wartime prices and trade board issued a further order, No. A-505, applicable only to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. It controlled the purchase, shipment and sale of the empty beer bottles in the two provinces. * Prior to that they were sold without any control from the wartime prices and trade board and could be shipped out of the province. I am not objecting to that order if it were administered in the way it was intended so as to give producers of beer in those two provinces their requirements. New Brunswick administered this order in the spirit in which it was issued. They recognize nine dealers in the province, namely, Thomas Buraglia, Bathurst; A. Freedman and Son, Saint John; J. Omer Guidry, Campbellton;

Hachey Bros., Chatham; Fred Levesque, Edmundston; W. G. McIntyre, Saint John; J. A. Robichaud, Rexton; G. Rubenstein, Chatham, and Harry Ruch, Moncton. In Nova Scotia no such condition prevailed. The orders of the wartime prices and trade board have been grossly abused, creating a monopoly under the control and for the profit and patronage of a notoriously partisan political friend of the government of Nova Scotia, namely, W. B. Moriarty, for the whole mainland of Nova Scotia. Complaint was made to me. About three weeks ago, after several efforts, I got in touch with the chairman of the board, Mr. Donald Gordon, over the telephone. I told him that I was getting complaints and as a member of parliament I would like to get some information and justification for the order. He said that he had had complaints ad nauseam, that he was leaving the matter to the authorities in Nova Scotia to justify and that he did not wish to discuss it with me.
I have been before the public for twenty years as a member of the provincial legislature and of this house. I was a minister of a department for over eight years. In all that period I was never treated with such discourtesy by an official. I am not going to blame Mr. Gordon altogether, because I feel that he was put into a position that he could not justify, and that, therefore, he did not wish to discuss it. That is the only explanation I can give of his treatment of me. I told him that I was a member of parliament and that I wanted information in order to understand the complaint. After that I put certain questions on the order paper and asked for the return of all correspondence, which I have received and been able to look over to-day. It was brought down by the parliamentary assistant to the minister yesterday. He very kindly spoke to me about it and asked me if the information in the answers to the questions and in the return were what I wanted. They are what I wanted but I have not had time to stud}'' them fully. I did notice, however, that in some of the correspondence reference is made to other correspondence on certain dates, and that correspondence is not on the file. At a later time I shall be able to go over it and see what additional information I - require. I assume that the parliamentary assistant to the minister will see that I get it.
There is in this return of correspondence over eighty copies of correspondence and I have not had an opportunity to examine it thoroughly. I am now going to make a summary. First, there is the Minister of Finance. He is in charge. I understand he has general

War Appropriation

Finance
oversight of the wartime prices and trade board. I do not hold him responsible but I believe that he is being duped. Next, is the wartime prices and trade board under the chairmanship of Mr. Donald Gordon. Third in line of responsibility of handling these beer bottles in Nova Scotia is the chief commissioner of the liquor commission in the person of Mr. A. S. Mahon, of Halifax, who was a political appointee. As such I have no quarrel with him if he were administering the affairs of the province in peace time. But in administering a war order in war time under these circumstances, to prostitute the wartime prices and trade board as he has done, acting for Mr. Moriarty, I say it is discreditable to this war parliament, and I ask that he be dismissed from that position and that someone in whom the province of Nova Scotia and the country has confidence be appointed to administer that responsibility. I would suggest that Mr. Lee be appointed. He represents the board in Nova Scotia. I would favour his appointment or that of any capable man who has some sense of responsibility, free from political bias. W. Stanley Lee is the prices and supply representative of the wartime prices ' and trade board, Cunard building, Halifax, Nova Scotia. He would be satisfactory, or any man irrespective of politics who would administer these duties in time of war with some sense of responsibility. The fourth man in the line appointed by Mr. Mahon is Mr. W. B. Moriarty, president of the Provincial Bottle Exchange, Limited, who played outright politics and favouritism and does not represent that he does anything else. He does it for profit and he is doing it under the wartime prices and trade board. I hold the Minister of Finance responsible and I hold Mr. Gordon responsible. I hold all those who are over him responsible. This man Moriarty undertook to give instructions of a dictator as soon as the order was passed to those who were handling bottles in Nova Scotia. In New Brunswick they did not do that. They worked with those who had been in the business, but not so Nova Scotia. He made use of this order to put a legitimate dealer, with whom Mr. Moriarty was not in sympathy, out of business, a man who had the previous year shipped up to 200,000 dozen empty beer bottles out of the province and who the year prior to that had sold 170,000 dozen altogether, of which 110,000 were marketed in Nova Scotia and 60,000 exported. I have the exact figures of what was shipped during seven months of the year 1942, and it bears out the statement that I have made.
Now, when this order was put into effect Moriarty telephoned or got in contact with
this firm, John Ross and Sons, that had been in the business which I have just described in Truro and told them that they were not per mitted to ship any more. They had at thal time 50,000 or 60,000 dozen bottles on hand. They had a carload loaded on the rails, but they could not get a permit to ship that one carload. They had to unload it, and they were forced to do so in the name of the wartime prices and trade board order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Moriarty is not an official of the wartime prices and trade board.

He is, when they recognize him. The Minister of Finance recognizes Mr. Donald Gordon; Mr. Donald Gordon recognizes Mr. Mahon; Mr. Mahon appoints Mr. Moriarty as his representative on the mainland of Nova Scotia, and therefore I hold the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant responsible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall reply in due course, when my hon. friend has finished, but I am just pointing out that Mr. Moriarty is not an official of the wartime prices and trade board.
He is the only man allowed to buy bottles on the mainland. He has a monopoly.

Mr. Ross
wanted to come to an understanding with the wartime prices and trade board; he wanted to abide by the rules, and he endeavoured to obtain recognition. He continued to buy from his clients and accumulated a supply of almost one hundred thousand dozen bottles. He had $40,000 invested in these bottles and could not dispose of them. The question arose of what he was to do with them; he either had to go into bankruptcy or knuckle down; accordingly he knuckled down and came to terms with this man Moriarty in order to ship his stock on hand. This was shipped out of the province to Moriarty's orders at a profit to Moriarty of from $50 to $100 a car. His stock on hand ran to twenty-five cars or more at that time, with a very much larger quantity purchased afterwards. This man Moriarty never had to raise his finger, except to telephone and give shipping orders; yet he got a rake-off of $50 to $100 a car.
This order was passed under the plea that the bottles were required for the brewers in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That may be partly so. Mr. Ross was prepared to ship to the firm in Halifax, through Mr. Moriarty, but he wanted to ship out of the province to his own customers. Prior to this order A-505 he had been shipping a large quantity out of
War Appropriation-Finance

the province direct to brewers. When the order was put into effect he was completely cut off from that business and he either had to hold his goods or sell them to the firm of Moriarty. I have some correspondence here, giving further particulars with respect to this business. Prior to the original order of 1942 Mr. Ross was selling to firms in central Canada, and was sending a considerable quantity to Halifax by truck, handing them over to Mr. Moriarty. He was satisfied to do that, at a reduced price; he was getting a return load coming back, and the business was reasonably satisfactory. But while he was buying in his own territory he was being undermined and interfered with by Mr. Moriarty's other buyers. That was not sufficient to put him out of business, so that Mr. Moriarty or Mr. Mahon or those in authority were able to have this war-time order put into effect. I am now going to read from a letter dated June 26, 1942, to show the dictatorial manner in which this man Moriarty usurped the right to control the beer bottle business in Nova Scotia. The letter is addressed to Mr. Harry Ross, of John Ross and Sons, and I need not read it all:
I want it definitely understood from this date that you are not to shi.p any bottles out of Nova Scotia and I want you to let me know how many .bottles you have on hand at the present time. I don't wish to have any unpleasantness with you, and I ask your cooperation trusting it will work out to our mutual advantage.
J. B. Moriarty,
President.
On the letterhead is the "Provincial Bottle Exchange". Here is another letter dated June 17, 1942, I presume from the manager of Canadian Breweries of Quebec, telling the Ross firm that they require more empty beer bottles and indicating that they are prepared to continue to carry on business with them. I need not read the letter; it is available if needed.

speechtext: Are these letters being tabled?
The hon. member will hand them to you.

Yes. I have a copy of a letter from Mr. Mahon to Mr. Rosenberg, deputy administrator of used goods, dated June 30, 1942, one paragraph of which reads:
From the information I have Mr. Ross has 0nly recently been active in the bottle business, and I really do not think we are doing him any injustice in appointing him a B dealer-
That is a dealer who has to sell his bottles at forty cents a dozen as against the ceiling price of forty-five cents a dozen.
-as I do not agree with his statement that the bottle business is his mainstay..

From whom?

It is from R. Geddes addressed to Mr. A. S. Mahon. I quote:
Dear Mr. Mahon:
a Developments in the functioning of our order A-505 respecting empty beer bottles, have been such that the question of rescinding it and allowing the trade in these goods to return to the basis on which it was conducted prior to tlie adoption of our order arises.
The order was instituted, as you know, to ensure an equitable distribution of empty beer bottles collected in your province and in New Brunswick and, in particular to ensure that the supply for local breweries was not drawn away to central Canada markets where excessive demands for beer and potentially limited production of new bottles were then indicated. It was not intended that the order would become an instrument for immobilizing hundreds of thousands of bottles in the hands of a collector or collectors and place them in storage where they are neither at the disposal of your local brewers nor of the central Canada brewers.
That has, however, happened, not because of the order itself but of the administration of it-
I would emphasize that-"not because of the order itself but because of the administration of it."
-which has become entwined with informal arrangements for bottle collection and distribution which had been operative in your province but were neither recognized nor ratified by this order of ours. The order was designed, as mentioned above, to ensure equitable distribution of bottles and, since it is not doing so, but rather achieving the reverse, the question of rescinding it logically arises.
If the situation which now prevails in respect of these bottles is carried to its ultimate, huge stocks of bottles are going to be withdrawn from use and brewers' stocks will have to be replenished by the manufacture of new bottles, with attendant but unnecessary wastage of labour and materials in doing so. We do not wish to see this development carried further and to have one or more dealers become the unwilling hoarders of bottles.
We wished to notify you of our plans for rescinding the order before proceeding with them. Hie supply situation apparently no longer required the control which the order imposed; while these huge stocks have been accumulating, no evidence of shortages in your province have come to our attention. If it is demonstrated tbat some measure of control is still necessary, we shall, of course, reconsider the decision. We will await your advice in this connection until March 1st.

On the file there are letters from Mr. Mahon there may be others, I do not know-pleading with Mr. Geddes not to rescind order A-505 which they were administering under such dictatorial powers for the political and financial benefit of some people in the province and certainly not in the spirit of a war-time order that should have the support of everybody in the country, not as a government measure to be administered by partisans, but as an order to be administered in such a manner as to meet the wishes and command the confidence of the people of Canada. The order should command the confidence of those who have contributed to enlistments in our armed forces; it should command the confidence of those who have invested in victory bonds and of those who supported the plebiscite vote. That is what it should do, rather than be for the benefit of those who have for years past administered anything over which they had control on the basis of the greatest possible political advantage. I am sorry to have taken up all this time dealing with beer bottles, upon which I am no authority.

The gravamen of the charge made by the hon. member for Cumberland is not against the principle of the order of the wartime prices and trade board but against its operation. In the return made to the questions asked by the hon. member for Cumberland, which was brought down yesterday and from which he has quoted some portions, it is indicated that the purpose of administrator's order A-505 of December 7, 1942, signed by the administrator of used goods, Mr. Godfrey, and approved by Mr. Gordon, was to keep used beer bottles needed for the use of brewers in the maritimes in the maritime provinces and thus avoid the shipment of empties back to Ontario and Quebec and the shipment of additional quantities of new bottles to the maritime brewers. The order applied not only to Nova Scotia but to New Brunswick. For some reason unknown to me, and possibly with the 'best intentions, in each case the chairman of the provincial liquor commission was appointed the representative of the wartime prices and trade board. In the case of New Brunswick it was Mr. R. G. Fulton, and in the case of Nova Scotia, Mr. A. S. Mahon.
For this purpose only?

For this
purpose only.

Very natural.

I do not think it was natural; I am surprised it was done. As far as Mr. Fulton was concerned, I think he operated the order, not only to the satisfaction of the suppliers but to the satisfaction of the brewers and the public generally. He recognized all the established dealers in New Brunswick who were collecting beer bottles. I assume that he saw to it that the two New Brunswick breweries, which by the way are operated by the Oland family, who also operate one if not the two breweries in Halifax-it is an old family custom-were properly looked after. Permits were issued to each of the nine dealers to sell the breweries beer bottles. There has been no complaint either as to prices or otherwise.
However, in Nova Scotia, a different policy was adopted by Mr. Mahon. In the first place, Mr. Mahon recognized only one A class dealer, his friend, Mr. Moriarty, who was given a monopoly. The gravamen of the charge made by the hon. member for Cumberland is that a monopoly was placed in the hands of the Provincial Bottling company, if that is its name, owned and controlled by Mr. Moriarty and his friends, and that the other dealers who collected bottles in Nova Scotia were refused licences to sell direct to the breweries.
On the mainland of Nova Scotia.

I must
limit my statement to the mainland of Nova Scotia. In Cape Breton my old friend Myer Cohen, who used to be a Conservative when he lived in Saint John and who became a Liberal after he went to Nova Scotia, was able to carry on. He was a very good worker in the ranks of the Conservative party when he lived in Saint John, but he is now a Liberal since he got this concession from the government.

speechtext:
There is no difference
between you anyway.

Maybe
there is not, but you are a poor judge. You are not going to interrupt me by saying that. As I say, a monopoly was created in Nova Scotia, and no one could ship a single bottle out of that province although bottles were accumulating that were not actually required by the breweries. That is one point that I wanted to make. Mr. Mahon refused to allow other dealers to ship surplus bottles out of the province to the breweries in central Canada which actually required them. The correspondence shows that they were asking for them. These breweries felt that they had not had their fair share of the distribution. That is the first charge, that a monopoly was created.
The effect of creating that monopoly was this. The selling price of these bottles was forty-five cents a dozen-I can be corrected if I am wrong-and Moriarty, without any investment of capital, without doing anything except using the telephone and keeping his books, was able to buy bottles from these people for forty cents. He thus had a rake-off of five cents a dozen, which is substantial because it would amount to from $60 to $100 a car. Not content with his monopoly, not content with his unearned profit or increment, lie went out into the territory and bid against the other dealers for surplus bottles whicbthey could not buy at the price at which they had to sell to him. That is to say, he was offering forty cents a dozen which was all the other men could get. He was assured of a profit without any sense of loss because he had a sure customer. All he had to do was to turn over the bottles to the brewers at forty-five cents a dozen and pocket the profit.
I am not going to blame Mr. Donald Gordon for the inception of the theory on which he was proceeding. He wanted to conserve beer bottles for the maritime breweries. It is the instrument which he set up to deal with the matter about which complaint is made. This has had the result of driving honest dealers out of business, while his chosen instrument- a common phrase in this house at times-was given a monopoly which gave him anywhere from $50,000 to $100,000 a year. I hope he is paying income tax on that profit. If he is not, someone ought to direct the attention of the Department of National Revenue to the fact.
The time arrived shortly after when the situation which made necessary the order was no longer in effect. Because of the large number of newcomers to the province, especially to Halifax, and the two great military camps, there was always a surplus of bottles after a certain period of time after the order was passed. This correspondence indicates that there was no longer any necessity for the order, and responsible officials here in Ottawa sought to have it rescinded and indicated their intention of so doing.
But they were probably over-persuaded by Mr. Mahon not to do any such thing but to continue the arrangement he had made, under which his friend Mr. Moriarty obtained a profit of five cents a dozen on all the empty beer bottles which he chose to take and which he supplied to the brewers in Halifax, shipping the rest out of the province. He had a monopoly not only for the local market but for the surplus which he acquired from the sources I have indicated and which he shipped out of the province. The whole thing became
War Appropriation-Finance

a racket; there is no doubt about that, and it ought to be ended if it has not been ended before. I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that if he becomes seized of all the facts he will recommend to Mr. Gordon that the order be rescinded forthwith, taking care that a sufficient number of bottles are provided for the breweries of Nova Scotia. But let them, buy the bottles by contract from the recognized dealers. They will get the beer bottles all right; there is no doubt about that, and the ceiling price will be adhered to. I have heard no complaint about the price. The complaint is that these men are no longer able to deal directly with the brewers who must deal through one funnel and pay a toll to the proprietor of that funnel. That is wrong if it be a fact, and I have no doubt it is a fact.
What should happen is this. The order should long ago have been rectified and permits should have been issued to these men to deal directly with the brewers and ship their surplus out of the province. That would be fair play and British justice.
I said in my opening statement that I have no fault to find with the underlying intent of the order at the time it was made, because no doubt it was passed on representations that were made by responsible people, we will say, to the wartime prices and trade board that there was a scarcity or threatened scarcity of beer bottles in Nova Scotia. That situation has been rectified. It no longer obtains. The necessity for the order therefore no longer exists. Certainly by the cancellation of that order a great injury to the local dealers on the mainland of Nova Scotia will have been rectified.
The plea I make to the minister is that he ask Mr. Donald Gordon to review the whole position and to put it on the same basis as the operation in New Brunswick, namely, that all the established dealers collecting empty beer and liquor bottles in Nova Scotia be recognized; that permits be issued to them; that they be allowed to sell at the ceiling price to the brewers direct, and not through one chosen instrument as is done in Nova Scotia, and that they be allowed to export the surplus to breweries in any part of Canada. That is a fair statement of the position as it ought to be and as it exists in New Brunswick, where there is not a single complaint so far as I am aware. That is the situation as it ought to be in Nova Scotia, where there is nothing but turmoil in this business owing to the fact that unwittingly-
I go that far-Mr. Gordon allowed himself to be led into this position. No wonder he refers to this beer bottle question, with all 	.
the complaints he has received, as nauseating. I have no doubt that it would be nauseating to any man who had found that he had made a mistake and did not rectify it. If we are going into the record of hon. members of this House of Commons I should like to have a little time and I would go into the hon. member's record, too. If he wants some exposure on the floor of this House of Commons, I will expose him.

That is the information

I want to read to the committee section 4, subsection 2, which deals with Nova Scotia and which is in identical terms with subsection 1 dealing with New Brunswick. This is what the section says:
Except with the permission in writing, of the chief commissioner of the Nova Scotia liquor commission, no person shall
(a)	purchase any used beer bottles which are now or which are hereafter located in the province of Nova Scotia for shipment to any other province;-
In other words, that prohibits the purchase for export.
(b)	ship or cause to :be shipped any such bottles to any other province;

Then the hon. member might tell the committee that these brewers are not allowed to purchase except through certain channels.

Certainly there is nothing
in the order of the wartime prices and trade board to that effect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

Let me finish my statement. As I say, the wartime prices and trade board was interested in adopting an order which would prevent the waste of shipping facilities
War Appropriation-Finance

by sending bottles to central Canada and shipping bottles back to Nova Scotia. That was the purpose of this order, and it did not create any monopoly in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick as far as the sale of used beer bottles in those provinces was concerned. If any such monopoly exists it was not created by any order of the wartime prices and trade board. The board is not charged with administering the Nova Scotia liquor commission; or the New Brunswick liquor commission; and identical provisions were established for New Brunswick. The commissioner of the New Brunswick liquor control board has the same powers as the commissioner of the Nova Scotia liquor control board; and the only effect of that order, as far as creating a monopoly is concerned, is that the chief commissioner of the government liquor control board is empowered to say who can export used beer bottles from Nova Scotia. The wartime prices and trade board is completely justified in taking the word of the responsible head of the government liquor commission, who, I assume, is charged with the distribution of beer in the province. It has done so in Nova Scotia and has done the same thing in New Brunswick. I would point out what has not been made clear in any of the previous speeches, that there is no restriction on any dealer in Nova Scotia collecting used beer bottles and selling them to either of the two breweries in Nova Scotia, but he cannot export them without a permit. That is the position as far as the wartime prices and trade board is concerned. The hon. member for Cumberland read a letter from Mr. Geddes, chief of the supply division, I think dated February 22, 1943, in which-

Would the hon. member not agree with my statement that the entire stock of almost one hundred thousand dozen bottles which had been accumulated by Ross was shipped out of the province by order of Mr. Moriarty, and not used by the brewers of Nova Scotia?

I do not know anything about the details of how they were shipped; I am dealing with the order passed by the wartime prices and trade board to control a situation which, as I indicated at the outset of my remarks, was resulting in the inefficient use of transportation facilities. provincial liquor commission, whether the administration in power happens to be Liberal or Conservative. He is the man responsible for the sale and distribution of these beverages, and I suggest that he is a perfectly proper person to whom the wartime prices and trade board should go for information on these matters.
