speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the parliamentary
assistant is through I should like to bring one or two points to the attention of the committee in connection with this matter. Perhaps the hon. gentleman is carrying his argument a little far when he suggests that this order is being continued in effect because of the problem which exists in regard to the transportation of empty bottles from Nova Scotia to the central provinces.
One instance which will at once disprove any such contention is the fact that while this order was apparently being kept in effect for that purpose, at the same time, the firm which is referred to as the Moriarty firm-I am using that only as a matter of distinction from the others-had shipped empty beer bottles from Nova Scotia to the central provinces and apparently with the consent and by the authority of the Nova Scotia liquor commission or its head, who had been given a special job under the wartime prices and trade board. I point that out to the parliamentary assistant because it fairly well shatters the argument that this order was put into effect for the purpose of conserving transportation between central Canada and Nova Scotia. The fact that there was considerable shipment of empty bottles from Nova Scotia to central Canada also, I think, adds substantial weight to the case put up by the hon. member for Cumberland.
At one time there may have been some justification for order A-505; but, as time went on, the effect of transportation of this product and these commodities from Nova Scotia to central Canada fairly well dispensed with the necessity of continuing the order. That having been the case, the committee must look for the reasons why the order was continued, and those reasons have been supplied by those who know much more about the matter than those of us who have not made a close study of it. As the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for
York-Sunbury pointed out, it would have the effect of giving the head of the Nova Scotia liquor commission the right to point his finger to one particular dealer and to say, "Only you may deal with other provinces by way of export of this commodity from Nova Scotia." That had the effect-and I say this in an endeavour to argue the case fairly with all concerned-of establishing a continued monopoly in so far as the man who was pointed to by the head of the liquor commission is concerned.
May I say to the parliamentary assistant, I can understand why the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board would feel very sick, as he said, of telephone calls and being bothered with the matter, because it seems to me, whatever may have been the underlying reason, and I am ascribing no untoward reasons or untoward influence with respect to this matter, that when the wartime prices and trade board saw fit to appoint the head of the liquor contmission of Nova Scotia-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am dealing with Nova Scotia, because apparently in New Brunswick they carry on their affairs a little differently and, perhaps, a little more satisfactorily, in regard to their empty beer bottles. In any event, I have no desire to join issue with my good friend from Halifax in what he has said to-night. In the appointment of the head of the liquor commission to a responsible position on the wartime prices and trade board, and the minister having some knowledge, as he must have had, that there was a situation such as this existing in Nova Scotia, what actually happened was that the fingers of the wartime prices and trade board and of this government as well were burned because of the situation that developed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not say that in any offensive way. I am simply trying to explain the situation that actually exists because the delivery into the hands of the Nova Scotia liquor control commission of the powers of the wartime prices and trade board with respect to this matter, whether the dominion government likes it or not, placed the whole situation, from, the point of view of the government, right into Nova Scotia politics, and it is because of that that the weakness of the whole arrangement becomes so apparent. I rose to ask the parliamentary assistant to investigate the matter thoroughly, and I suggest that if he does so he will find that there is no longer any real necessity for order A-505 remaining in effect. Whatever may have
War Appropriation-Finance

been its advantages in the beginning, it now operates against the public interest. That I have gathered as I have listened to the convincing arguments advanced in this debate.

If we are now through dealing with second-hand beer bottles, perhaps we can return to the cup that cheers but does not inebriate. A year ago I took up the question of the increase in the price of tea, coffee and milk sold in restaurants in this city and elsewhere across the country. That question is still pricking the conscience of the minister and some members of the wartime prices and trade board as well, because only yesterday, in another discussion, the minister brought up the question again and told us that because the price of meats and other foods had gone up in restaurants they allowed an increase in the price of tea and coffee. This, I believe, was thrown out as a sop to some of the organized restaurant keepers and it did not take into consideration the effect it had on certain victims. I bring this question up now because to-day we have an increased supply of tea and coffee. There is no shortage of either of :hese commodities. Nor is there any shortage of milk at the present time. Prior to the time the order was put into effect we could go into a restaurant and get one or two or three cups of tea or coffee or we could get additional milk and we did not have to pay any extra money for the coffee we drank.
At the present time we are told that because prices of meat and other foods have gone up, an increase of five cents on tea, coffee and milk has been allowed. Very little consideration, however, has been given to the effect which this has on certain people. The number of people who can afford to eat some, of the more expensive foods, including strawberries-something that was discussed yesterday-are now getting away from the increased cost of meals, but those who have to use tea or coffee or milk, and peihaps a muffin or something else for breakfast, or lunch, or perhaps the evening meal, are paying the additional cost. I do not think this is fair, and I ask once more that some consideration be given the matter, because you are penalizing the wrong persons. You are penalizing the poor for the benefit of the rich. If the price of meat has gone up in restaurants, then let the people who have the benefit of the better foods pay the additional prices, and let those who have a cup of tea or coffee, or a glass of milk, and who, in some cases, at the end of the month, after paying their taxes, have little left to buy meat and some of the good foods, be allowed to get their tea and coffee without paying extra.
There is another matter I want to call to the attention of the wartime prices board.

Several complaints have been made to me that in the chart sent out by the board showing the different cuts of animals sold over the butcher's block, the price always quoted is that of the top quality beef or pork, and it does not make any difference whether it is the top grade that is being sold by the butcher or an old milk cow that has raised half a dozen children for some farmer, the price is the same. I think some consideration should be given to this and some attempt made to create a price range according to the grade of meat sold. If you go into a restaurant and order a ham or beef or some other kind of sandwich I think you will find out that what I am saying is correct. If you get your teeth into it you will be lucky to get them out again, and the price will be the same as though you were getting top-grade meat.
I suppose you would leave false teeth in?

False teeth are better than none at all. If you have poor teeth, false teeth would be preferable. I do not know whether it is necessary to go on any further, but I ask the wartime prices and trade board to give this matter some consideration. I do not make this plea on my own behalf; I make it on behalf of some of our lower paid workers who, I am informed by those who work in restaurants, have not enough to eat when pay day comes around or for two or three days before. They are unable to buy *a decent meal; all they can get is a bowl of soup with muffins or something of that kind. We should take away the penalties from those who are not able to bear them and place them where they properly belong, namely, upon those who eat meat and other foods that have gone up in price.
Get a smaller car.

I like to ride in a comfortable car.
My last complaint is in reference to maple syrup. To my mind, producers of maple syrup have been greatly interfered with this year. I buy maple syrup in six-gallon lots. That required twenty-four sugar coupons, but after I got my coupons together I had to drive from one end of the city to the other in order to get some sort of certificate to mail to the farmer producer, so that he could express my maple syrup. That was just a nuisance; it is one of the many things that has interfered with maple syrup and other production and sale. I am quite sure that the same thing would apply to other commodities.
It has been said to-day that many of the officials in charge of the wartime prices and trade board regulations have had very little experience in dealing with the public or in dealing with the commodities under their control. This would not apply to all. I know many of them who are really big men, who have done a fine job, but on the other hand I would judge that many of them are more or less inexperienced. How they came to be taken on the staff I do not know.
Earlier in the day we were given the number of those employed1 by the wartime prices and trade board. I was just looking up the public accounts for 1943 and I notice it states that the number of employees drawing $2,400 a year and over was 4,769. It does not state how many were drawing less than $2,400. That is a tremendous staff. They may all be necessary, but I am undter the impression that this is just another case of governmental interference in business that cannot be controlled and where two men are employed when one is all that is needed.
I have always been an advocate of good salaries. The more a man makes, the more he
can buy. However, bpt I find that of that number of 4,769, between ninety-five and 1-00 were drawing from $4,000 to $5,000 a year; between twenty-five and thirty were drawing from $5,000 to $6,000; between twenty and twenty-five were drawing from $6,000 to $7,000; approximately five, if I have counted correctly in my hurry, were drawing between $7,000 and $8,000; another five were drawing between $8,000 and $9,000, and one was drawing over $10,000.
I have no doubt that the men in the high income brackets are A1 men. They must be or they would not be in those positions. Quite possibly their salaries are less than they should be, but in the aggregate it is a staggering payroll to anyone who has been connected with big business. I would like to compare this payroll with the payrolls of the New York Central, the General Electric or any one of those huge companies. I doubt if any of those companies has comparably such a colossal payroll, a payroll on which so many large salaries are paid. I am not going to find any fault with it because I like to hear of men getting good salaries. However, I ask this question: when the war is over, how is business to get its staffs back and have them comfortable and happy when they know that such salaries have been paid by the government during the war?
I have nothing further to say other than that I am not going to find any fault with any particular official. These men have had a strenuous time and they have done a very difficult job. I hope they have been doing the best they can, but I do know that the public everywhere are incensed because of regulations which do not seem to be sensible. There may be reasons for them, or for some of them, but the public are not conversant with them. I am thinking particularly of some of the things that were mentioned a short time ago such as buttons on coats, cuffs on trousers and so on. These are only small items in the aggregate. The amount saved in comparison with more or less reckless expenditures in scores of other directions does not commend itself to the public.

I sincerely hope
that the wartime prices and trade board can survive the attack that was made upon them with empty beer bottles to-night, strawberries yesterday, coal and so forth.
I have moved about the eastern part of the country probably as much as most members. I have had occasion to visit a great many points in four provinces within the last six or eight months, and I am satisfied that in general the people of Canada are supporting
War Appropriation-Finance

the government's measures and the controls established by the wartime prices and trade board.
I have conversed with many scores of small business men who complain of difficulty in getting all the goods they want and of many of the controls, but a great many of them have admitted quite frankly that but for the controls of the wartime prices and trade board they would probably not be able to get enough to sell, that the fact that they can remain in business under the conditions that prevail in war time is due to the quotas established by the board which entitle them to get goods to sell. I have no doubt that the small business men of the country realize that in times such as these, without those controls, the larger business concerns, the monopoly interests of this country, would have gained a much greater control of our business life than they now have.
I am confident that by and large the consumers of the country are grateful for the rationing which has been adopted. I think the majority of our people, certainly those with limited means, realize that they are enabled through the rationing regulations to get a portion of the goods that are available for sale. I think the general population throughout the country realizes that these controls have effected a stabilization of prices which has had an effect upon the rising cost of living. We have only to compare the cost of living to-day with the cost of living in the last war to realize that there are a great many benefits to be derived from these controls. I certainly hope that the criticism which we hear of the wartime prices and trade board will not have -the effect of releasing all these controls too quickly or of releasing too many of them too quickly. I think everyone who has given much consideration to the problems that will face us immediately after the war realize that, in the interests of the country generally, some of these controls will have to be maintained for some time after the war ends, regardless of which government is in power.
I have heard criticism of specific regulations of the wartime prices and trade board and criticism of the -administration of specific regulations. I realize, as I think most members of the house do, that in the early days of the board a great many of the positions in its organization were filled -possibly by party workers, were patronage jobs, -but I have not heard in more recent months nearly as much complaint along that line as I heard at the beginning.
The board has unquestionably made mistakes. I well recall how infuriated the small retail dealers were at some of the regulations
CMr. Noseworthy.]
that were imposed upon them in the early days of the board, regulations regarding the delivery of goods and so forth, but these I th-ink have been largely ironed out as time went on.
I remember being in the maritimes last fall when -the new order relating to dressed and undressed poultry came into effect. It was the talk of the whole of at least two of those provinces. I doubt if any government ever received so much criticism from among the farming people as did this government because of -that order. I was asked by a certain number of people to get in touch with the -prices board, but by the time I could get around to doing it I discovered that the regulation had been modified.
There was still a great deal of criticism regarding the deterioration of goods. People all across this country are not satisfied that the wartime prices and trade board or some other government agency is doing all that could be done to prevent that deterioration. I have gone into many towns where retail merchants have showed me articles which, while the price remains the same, have deteriorated until in their opinion they were not worth more than half the price at which the article formerly sold. I have had instances of that in dry goods stores in connection with articles of clothing, and in many other stores.
The hon. member for Davenport has called the attention of the committee to the situation regarding coal. Only last week in an eastern Ontario town several citizens showed me their coal bills for this last winter as compared with their coal bills for previous winters, showing how they had been forced to buy several tons of coal more than they had been in the habit of buying. They were complaining that the coal they got last year, although the price was pegged, was much inferior in quality to what they had been receiving in pr'evious years, and many of them were also complaining of light weight, that a ton of coal contained a great deal of water and much less coal than it formerly did.
One suggestion I would like to make to the parliamentary assistant is that if there is any possibility of simplifying the type of returns or of reducing the number of returns that have to be made by business men and firms to the wartime prices and trade board, any attempt in that direction will meet with the approval of vast numbers of people across this country.
I have seen restaurant keepers and hotel managers, particularly, sitting up to the wee hours of the morning trying to figure out how many cups of tea and coffee they sold, how many customers they served, how many pounds of this and that were disposed of

War Appropriation-Finance
during the day-all of which apparently had to be recorded on a set form and forwarded to the officials. If the people of Canada are to accept the regulations which the wartime prices and trade board has to introduce, any orders which have very little value except a nuisance value should be eliminated. I have been told-I should like to know from the parliamentary assistant whether it is true- that the forms which have to be filled out are to some extent affected by the requirements of United States authorities in similar situations; that in order to obtain priorities, in order to work in line with the Americans, our wartime prices and trade board must be able to show to the entire satisfaction of United States authorities that we have effective control over goods and services, and that our board can satisfy these authorities only by showing them returns similar to their own. I hope that this is not true. I hope also that the wartime prices and trade board can take some measures to simplify and reduce these returns.
Last year a return was brought down showing the number of dollar a year men employed by the wartime prices and trade board. I wonder whether there would be very much work involved in bringing that list up to date. I think it would be interesting to the committee to know whether we have fewer or more dollar a year men, and who are thus employed by the board. It seems to me that by this time it should have trained men of its own who are capable of managing the affairs of the board, and that it should be possible to get along with fewer of these dollar a year men.
One further suggestion. Probably some of the criticisms or causes of criticism arise from the fact that there is not on the councils of the wartime prices and trade board adequate representation of the interests affected. That, I believe, was brought out in yesterday's debate. I believe it applies to a great many instances, that those responsible for the regulations pertaining to particular lines of business, particular commodities, are often familiar with large enterprises dealing in the commodity but not with the point of view of the small business man. 1 would like, if it would not involve too much work, to have that list of dollar a year men brought up to date.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have here the figures for both years. As a matter of fact this information was given in answer to a question of the hon. member for York East on May 18. The number of employees of the wartime prices and trade board serving full time without
remuneration on March 31, 1943, was 293, and on March 31 of this year, 329; approximately the same, or rather, over thirty more.
As to the simplifying of forms, I can assure my hon. friend that a constant effort is being made to do that. On the other hand, the board is carrying on a complicated and difficult operation, and has to have a considerable amount of accurate information in order to carry out its responsibility properly, and for that reason it has to require that a good many forms be filed. A committee of the board is constantly working on the question, reviewing these forms and endeavouring to see that they are made as simple as they can be, I do not know with what degree of success; but in any event, a constant effort is being made to do that.
As to similarity of forms with those in force in the United States, I am advised that there is no real justification for that suggestion. There is this point that in connection with textile supplies, in particular, we are dependent upon United States supplies now for priorities and so forth; consequently we try to make our application forms and that sort of thing conform as closely as possible to those in use in the United States. Possibly that is what my hon. friend had in mind when he referred to that point.
The hon. member for Davenport raised one or two questions in connection with coal and gasoline. The question of supplies of coal, as he knows, is under the Department of Munitions and Supply. The price ceiling is fixed and enforced by the wartime prices and trade board. I have heard that there has been some deterioration in the quality of the coal which we have been getting lately. I have not noticed it in the case of my own coal, but that is perhaps no fair test. As to gasoline, again I do not know. The question of supply, as the hon. member is aware, is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and so far as I know the price has not varied since September or October, 1941.
The quality has, though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I am particularly fortunate, but I have not personally noticed any variation. I drive a very light car, and I think I get at least twenty miles and sometimes twenty-five miles a gallon in the country at the lower speeds at which we drive. I am sure the hon. member for Davenport does not drive at any excessive speeds.

I try to keep within the law.

War Appropriation-Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There may be some deterioration in the quality of gasoline, and it is perfectly true that the price is the same.
On the question raised by the hon. member about maple syrup, I can sympathize a good deal with his views, because I was bom and brought up in the part of Quebec which produces more and better maple syrup than anywhere else-[DOT]	-
Not "better"; perhaps "more".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-that is, the eastern townships. Being familiar with the processes of maple syrup making, and having bought and sold it for many years, I can sympathize with his views, and I heard a lot from my friends in the eastern townships regarding what they felt were the unnecessary restrictions upon the sale and distribution of maple syrup this year. Of course the reason, rightly or wrongly, for these restrictions was that maple syrup, maple butter and maple sugar were classed with what we call "sweet spreads", which include honey and jam; they are alternatives to these particular commodities, which, as my hon. friend knows, are rationed, and it Was felt that it would be unfair to allow maple products to go unrationed.
It would mean that distribution would not approach anything like a fair one; that people who were near the sources of supply or knew where to go would get the lion's share of the product and it would not be available for the general public. I am advised, and that is confirmed by what I learned out in this beautiful part' of Quebec to which I refer, the eastern townships, the maple sugar crop was good this year and apparently it has moved into consumption fairly smoothly. The selling price was higher than last year and I am told was sufficient to give a good return to the producer for his maple syrup. I am not going to assume the role of a prophet. I hope when the time arrives for the sugar crop next year it will not be necessary to ration this delicious commodity. I am sure that if it is necessary the sugar producers will put up with the relatively moderate inconvenience that they suffered this year and that those of us who, like the hon. member for Davenport, are very fond of this product, will also be willing to go to a little extra trouble to be sure that we procure it.
My hon. friend raised the question of salaries. I am not going into the details of the salaries now, but I wish to say to the committee that I do not consider the salaries paid by the wartime prices and trade board

to be in any way out of line with the salaries paid for comparable service in private business or in any other section of the community.
On July 7 of last year the Minister of Finance in answer to a question gave a breakdown in certain groups of persons in receipt of salaries in the employ of the board. While I have not a similar break-down here I am informed it has not changed substantially since that time. On July 7 of last year there was no one on the board receiving in excess of $8,500 a year.
In what year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In July of last year. I think that statement still holds good to-day. There is no one in receipt of a salary of more than $8,500 a year. As the committee knows, the chairman of the board is the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada and is on loan to the board.
The name I had in mind was D. G. MacKenzie. He is down for $10,400.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, I am informed that the gentleman named by the hon. member for Davenport was engaged on a special fee basis in the past. He still works for the board but at a very much lower scale of remuneration.
I have only the public accounts to go by.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And that is the only case. As I say, there is no one receiving a salary in excess of $8,500 a year. In the bracket from $5,000 to $8,500, there were forty-three. I am giving the committee the general picture. In the bracket from $3,000 to $4,000 there were 174; in the bracket from $2,000 to $3,000 there were 683; the remainder, those receiving $2,000 and under number 3,723, making a total of 4,965. The total to-day is some 5,100, and I doubt whether any are receiving high salaries; there may be one or two, but the majority of the increased number are in the lower income brackets, additional inspectors, enforcement officers and so on.
I do not find fault. I was asking for the number. Did the parliamentary assistant give the number receiving $8,000, $7,000 and $6,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. I said there were none receiving over $8,500 a year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
From $5,000 to $8,500 there were forty-three. I have not any smaller break-down, but in the bracket from $5,000 to $8,500 there were forty-three. I think my hon.

War Appropriation-Finance
friend and the committee are aware that some of those officers are performing exceedingly difficult and responsible duties. Not only that, but a great many of them have been lent to the board by their own private employers. They are not serving as dollar a year men. What is happening is that they are being paid the salary which they were receiving from their private employers. In most of those cases the employer continues to pay his own employee and is reimbursed by the board for the amount of the salary.
They take it out of the excess profits tax when they pay their taxes. It is the same thing exactly as the government paying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Of course it is the same thing as the government paying. I am not questioning that for a moment. I am simply pointing out that these men are not taking on a government job as a life job, as permanent civil servants. They have come here to do this as a war job. They are doing it at the same salary they were receiving from their private employer. The private employer loses the benefit of their service and he is neither ahead of nor behind the game. He is simply reimbursed for the salary.
It is hardly fair to say they are dollar a year men.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I did not say they were. In fact I prefaced what I said by saying they are not dollar a year men. The figures I have given for men serving without remuneration do not include men in the category to which I was referring. I made a statement that a great many of the men on the prices board included in the category of receiving, let us say, $5,000 to $8,500 a year, are men who have been lent temporarily to the board by their employers and are being paid the same salary that they would have continued to receive had they stayed in their own private business.
What types of positions do those men occupy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Administrators, chiefs of divisions. If the hon. member will look at the report of the wartime prices and trade board which I. tabled early in January he will see there a list of the principal officers of the board. The hon. member no doubt has a copy of the report before him. If he will look at pages 52 and 53 he will see a list there of the senior administrative officers of the board. For instance, the distributive trades coordination is headed by Mr. R. F. Chisholm.

Lent by whom?
100-215J

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The foods coordination is headed by Mr. K. W. Taylor, who is sitting in front of me. Metal and wood products coordination is headed by Mr. D. P. Cruik-shank, and so on.
The committee no doubt realizes that the wartime prices and trade board is carrying on in fact one of the biggest and most important businesses in this country. The decisions of the various administrators, as hon. members of the committee know, affect the lives and fortunes of every one of us. I know a good many of those men who have come here to serve in those capacities. I know they have done it not out of a desire to have any government job but out of an honest and sincere desire to help their country in war time. I am satisfied that they are not being overpaid, and I frankly feel that without some accurate knowledge hon. members should be hesitant-I am. not suggesting that the hon. member for Davenport took that line-to throw out the suggestion that these officials of the board are getting salaries which are out of line with the service they render. I am convinced from intimate personal knowledge that they are not.
They are getting the same salary that they were getting from their companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In some cases, but not in other cases, and there is no reason why they should not.
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to the minister how much refined sugar was damaged in Saint John while being held in storage by order of the wartime prices and trade board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid I have not the information at hand at the moment. I shall make a note of it and see if I can get the information.

I should like to make a few remarks with regard to what the hon. member for Davenport said with respect to the coal business. If anything, the standard of coal we received in the past year was as good as or better than we have received in Canada for a long time. The hon. member referred to twelve tons being burned by certain people, three tons more than a year ago. That is contrary to the experience of most people. Householders throughout Ontario who last year used six to eight tons of coal used one or two tons less this winter. That was reflected in the amount of coal we were obliged to import; and if it had not been for that coal we never would have been able to get through the winter. The hon. member for York South
War Appropriation-Finance

praised the wartime prices and trade board, but then came along with a couple of little digs about short weight, and the coal dealers selling water. I do not know where these gentlemen from the good city of Toronto get their coal, but if I lived there I would move out of Toronto and go some place where I could find honest coal dealers.

The hon. member may be quite right in saying that in the very mild winter through which we have just passed, one of the mildest in decades, some private houses in Smiths Falls may have used less coal, or may not have burned the coal, because in the first place it was hard to get and in the second place the price was high. However, I was speaking about people who owned apartment houses and duplexes, who had to supply the coal and whose tenants would not let the janitors cut down on the amount of coal used. I know what I said was correct. The next time I go to Smiths Falls I shall make a few inquiries and find out whether or not the coal sold by my hon. friend was so very fine.
I should like to know if order No. 184 of the wartime prices and trade board, prohibiting the setting up of new cooperative associations and organizations is still in effect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall have to get that information.

While the minister is looking that up I wish to draw to the attention of the committee some additional facts with regard to the beet-sugar industry. This afternoon the hon. member for Lambton gave a very fine review of the whole situation. He dealt with some of the assistance this government has given to the beet-sugar industry, but still I find that the quantity produced in 1943 was not as great as in 1942. For instance, the seeded area was 64,000 acres in 1942 and only 52,000 acres in 1943, and of course the yield was considerably less. This is an unfortunate situation, because some places in Canada are admirably suited to the production of sugar beets. There are the warmer areas of Ontario, the maritimee, the Okanagan valley and particularly places in Alberta where there is the maximum amount of sunshine, the richest soil, and good irrigation.
I want to make an earnest plea for an increase in the production of sugar from the home grown raw material, because we can produce these beets so well, particularly on irrigated land, and the benefits are so great. It will provide a great deal of employment in the immediate post-war period, which is surely an important coansi deration. A great deal of coal, a great deal of lime rock, a
TMr. Soper.]
great deal of coke; boxes, lumber, nails, bags, and various supplies of that kind are required. It produces freight for the railways and pays a good deal of money to farmers and factory workers. In giving evidence before a committee of this house the president of a large sugar company said that he knew of no industry which provided so much employment, not only for those actually handling the commodity but in connection with the materials used in the distribution of the product. Chemically there is no difference between cane sugar and beet sugar; they conform to exactly the same formula. At times it has been said that beet sugar has some disadvantages, but under modern refining methods there is absolutely no difference; I think that has been amply proven.
I particularly want to draw this to the attention of the parliamentary assistant because $35,000,000 has been spent in connection with irrigation in southern Alberta. Those irrigated districts are made much more profitable and the people on them are much more prosperous when there is a sugar-beet factory in the vicinity. There are such large areas as the eastern irrigation district around Brooks, and the western irrigation district farther west, where great quantities of beets could be produced, where the supply would be reliable, and where a sugar-beet factory would help greatly to assure the prosperity and stability of the people on the land. This industry means so much to the whole economic and social welfare of the people that I urge those in charge to give additional encouragement so that its benefits may be felt all through the Canadian economy, possibly in the way of freight rate reductions, tariff concessions, or further concessions in regard to the excise tax. I believe there are great possibilities for post-war employment and post-war reconstruction in making -use of water, which is now flowing down to the sea for irrigation purposes, and then stabilizing those irrigation districts with brct sugar factories.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to discuss the question of canned vegetables from the point of view of the orders which have restricted the amount reaching the public. On January 1 about nine and a quarter million dozen cans of vegetables were in the hands of canners and wholesalers, despite the fact that last year was less than an ample year of production. By April 1 that figure had been reduced to something under six and a quarter million dozen cans in the hands of canners and wholesalers, but that was a million dozen more than on the previous April 1, again

War Appropriation-Finance
despite the fact that last year's crop was not ample. It is true, I believe, that the restrictions were removed at the end of April, but the view I take is that the restrictions were maintained too long, because we have passed through those months of late winter when the consumer would have been glad to buy canned vegetables, and now that the restrictions are off and it is easier for the consumer to get the canned goods the fresh vegetables are coming onto the market.
I maintain that this is an unnecessary quantity of canned vegetables to have in the *hands of canners and wholesalers; and, with the restrictions having been kept on for so long, that quantity will probably remain in their hands instead of the quantity being reduced on the eve of what looks like a year of very big production. I know that one reason why these quantities have been held is to make sure that the very large quantities required for our forces and those of the allies shall be available. But I think that, with the experience of the past to guide the board, the restrictions have been kept on longer than necessary and that now there is an opportunity for the retailer to have rather more for disposal to the public than he should have. The public is moving on to buy the fresh vegetables and the stores of the wholesalers are having too many cans of vegetablese held on hand when it may be expected that a very large amount of canning will be forthcoming in this season.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will bring my hon. friend's comments to the attention of the board. As he has pointed out, the restrictions were removed on the 1st of May. It may be that they could or should have been removed a bit earlier, but as he himself has said, we often learn a good deal by experience. The point is that they are now removed. I suppose it is safe to say that they will not be reimposed unless it is felt that they are really necessary for the purposes suggested. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton asked about order 184, with regard to cooperatives going into business. Order 184 was subsequently amended by order 284 and finally amended on the 15th of this month by order 400. Order 184, originally imposed in November, 1942, imposed restrictions on the establishment, acquisition and extension of new business of all kinds, not only cooperatives but all new business, and when the original order was passed it was felt that there was need of a general curtailment of civilian activity to permit a more rapid expansion of war production. It was felt that the existing manufacturing and distributing facilities should be adequate, except in a few special cases, to handle available supplies
of civilian goods and that new productive activities should be devoted to meet the rapidly increasing war demands. To-day the war requirements remain heavy and must continue to have first call on production, but the rate of expansion of war production is not as great as during the period when orders 184 and 284 were in existence. Shortages continue to exist in many lines of civilian goods and these are unlikely to disappear for some time. However, there may be some types of civilian production that can be undertaken without interfering with the full war effort, and for other types preparations and plans must be made many months in advance of actual production. It was considered that decisions concerning the nature of so many new enterprises can be taken better by those who,desire to undertake these enterprises than by government agencies, and for these reasons the administration of order 284 is adapted in the light of conditions now applicable. As hon. members will no doubt have seen, the order was modified by order 400 to provide in effect that while new businesses must still get a licence to operate in order that a record may be kept of such new businesses, these licences will be granted, generally speaking, readily, almost as a matter of course, but on the understanding, as pointed out to the applicant when he gets his licence, that no assurance is given him in the granting of the licence that he will receive a quota of goods which may be in short supply. In other words, the licence to do business is more or less in the nature of a hunting licence, if I may so describe it. The applicant is free to go into business, but he must take a chance on being able to get an adequate supply of scarce goods and without reference to the board.
Does that apply to men discharged from the forces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
In other words, if they come back and try to set up in business, do they get no assurance of supplies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They have to get a licence the same as anyone else. I am advised in the case of returned men that an attempt is made to give them a quota where they are reestablishing a business in which they were engaged prior to joining the armed forces. In other words, they are put in a preferred position. They get their licence, but in addition to that an attempt is made to provide them with a quota if they were in a line of business which used scarce goods where a quota is required.

That is only in cases where they were in business before enlistment?
War Appropriation-Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
It would not apply to a young chap taking his discharge who had not been in business previously?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In that case he should endeavour to go into a line of business which does not require articles in short supply. I am referring to things like sugar, tea, and coffee, which are rationed on a quota basis, and that applies to a good many other things such as hardware, where there is definitely a short supply. In the interests of the general stability of the civilian economy, you cannot have people coming in and establishing new businesses in those particular lines where there is a definite shortage of stock-in-trade. That situation may correct itself very quickly. Those articles in short supply to-day, in four or six months' time may be in adequate supply; but I do not think it can be said as a definite statement that the returned man going into new business which he has not been in before, can be assured of a quota of stock-in-trade which is of a type in short supply.
Should he not have a preference to become established in a new business?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Every consideration will be given if he has been in that line of business before, and an attempt will be made to give him a quota. But where a particular type of commodity is definitely in short supply it is subject to the equitable distribution policy of the board, and it would simply create a chaotic condition in the distribution system to allow an unlimited or even a large number of new entrants into that particular field.
Suppose he wanted to go into canning farm produce?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is not in short supply.
I am referring to such things as hardware, steel products. These are definitely subject to the equitable distribution policy, and the wholesalers are obliged to allocate available supplies to their customers in an equitable manner in accordance with purchases in the base period. It is a form of rationing, of course.

I am obliged to the Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance for the assurance he gave a moment or two ago that there was no discrimination in the . policy of the board with respect to the issuing of licences for new businesses as between cooperatives and other organizations. That is a desirable provision, and I hope it will be followed out. I have a little experience in that regard and I can confirm what he

has said this evening in this matter. Listening to the discussion this afternoon and evening, I wonder what the general public's reaction will be. I am bound to say that when one goes about the country, the one feature of the government's domestic policy that is held up with greater acclaim than probably any other is the price control arrangements; and when we consider that along with the government's attempt to avoid inflation, I do not see how the two features of the government programme can be separated. But when we have a discussion in the House of Commons that seems to be a pretty general condemnation, certainly of many features of that programme, I wonder how the public will react to it. There have been cases where controls have not been exercised and we have experienced runaway prices. I refer particularly to used materials such as farm implements, tractors, used cars and things of that kind. In these cases it was found necessary to take action afterwards.
There are two classes in the community which are deserving of special mention in connection with the carrying out of the government's programme of price control and of rationing. Rationing is not a thing that everybody likes, but at least it is the idea of sharing so that everyone will have an opportunity of getting the goods that are available. The two classes which I think are particularly deserving of credit for what they have done are the retail country merchant and the automobile or gasoline dealer. From my observation these two classes of trades people have had more details to take care of and more trouble with respect- to looking after coupons and that kind of thing than anybody else. I am bound to say that in the part of the country from which I come there have been few of them who have had any complaints. In nearly every case they have come forward and said that they hoped the" government would extend its rationing or sharing policies to other articles that they were finding it difficult to handle. Those two classes certainly supported the government's efforts in the carrying out of these control measures.
I am surprised when I hear individual items picked out and condemned. If there are weaknesses in the policy they should be eliminated. I have met people from the United States who look upon our accomplishments with respect to price control as being splendid. They are particularly pleased with the enforcement of the control. You cannot have one without the other. I was talking to a business man in my town not so long ago and he put it in this way: having regard to the policy that was being carried on during

War Appropriation-Finance
this period of the war as compared with the last war, we are better off to-day. As he said after the last war when the inflationary period had got under way and the bubble had broken, business men simply went to their offices every morning to look at their inventories in order to see what their previous day's losses had been. That is the experience they had. The reaction of these business men is that every effort possible should be made to maintain the price ceiling so that business and the community generally will not get into a condition such as occurred at the close of the last war.
I think the country generally is behind the government's price control measures. Where weaknesses have been shown up, where individual items have been dealt with in a manner that was not the soundest, they have been rectified. It was a new policy and mistakes were bound to creep in, but I think the whole thing has been handled in a creditable manner.
I wish to say one thing more with respect to the general condemnation that has been made of many of the officials of the board and its policies. I have had some dealings with these gentlemen and I am bound to say that I have found them to be courteous; I found them to be men who knew their job; I found them to be men who were able to give me a reasonable explanation for the policy they were pursuing. I do not want anyone to think for one moment that I was able to persuade them to my point of view with respect to any particular matter we might happen to be discussing, but they were able to present the job they were doing in an understandable and reasonable manner. I think that much should be said for them. They are carrying out the policy in a practical and reasonable way; they are reasonable in their approach to it.
Would the parliamentary assistant give us the details of the recent amendment to the business order?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I described it, perhaps rather sketchily, a few minutes ago. It is order 400, which amends order 284, (which in turn amended order 184. Substantially the effect of the amending order is that while a licence is still required by a new entrant into business or for the expansion of existing business, it will be granted readily-I put it almost as a matter of course-but upon the understanding that the granting of a licence does not entitle an applicant to a quota of goods which are in short supply. In other words, the new entrant into business is given, as I put it, more or less
of a hunting licence. He is allowed to go into business as he would under normal conditions, but we have to issue a licence in order to have a record of the number of people in business. He gets his licence almost as a matter of course. If he is going into a business where inventories are in short supply he will have no assurance that he will be given a quota.
I am grateful to the parliamentary assistant for giving that explanation. There should be no diffi- ' culty in a man who wanted to open up a new coal mine getting a licence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: None whatever.
I am glad to hear that. There was an article in to-day's Journal-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is so far as wartime prices and trade board is concerned; I cannot answer for munitions and supply.

I am dealing with the wartime prices and trade board. This article refers to the shortage of coal, and it goes on to state that the coming winter may be one of the worst we have ever had as far as obtaining coal is concerned. I had a case which I took up with the wartime prices and trade board and the thing has been going along for some time. This man was trying to get a licence to operate a mine. He went to the board in Calgary and he was told that a licence could not be issued. This was a strip mine and he wanted to get it ready for this fall. He had spent a considerable amount of money in getting the mine ready for operation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This amending order 400 only came into effect on May 15 and perhaps the case to which the hon. member is referring was put forward before it came into force.

Probably that is true, because I have a letter from the wartime prices and trade board dated May 20 in which they state that a new amendment had just been made. That would correspond with what the parliamentary assistant has just said. As I say, this man had spent a considerable amount of money in stripping this mine, several thousand dollars, I understand. He went ahead with this mine on the advice of an official in the wartime prices and trade board. I am not going to give his name because I do not think that is necessary. He continued with his work until he reached the point where he decided there was no use in going ahead and spending more money. Yet we are told that there is to be a shortage of coal this winter. There should be no hesitancy
War Appropriation-Finance

in granting a licence to this particular individual. As far as I know he has not as yet been given a licence.
They are paying bonuses to open up new mines.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the hon. member will give me the name I shall have the matter looked into right away.
I will drop the parliamentary assistant a letter to-morrow giving him the details. I think this is a matter that can be cured with his assistance.

The matter to which I wish
to refer for a moment may not come strictly within the purview of the Department of Finance although, when one considers it from the point of view of rationing of food and the maintaining of food supplies, I believe it will be in order. I have had a number of complaints from ladies with respect to what has happened to their fruits in sealers. They claim that the rubber used last year in the jar rings was very poor. Many representations have been made with respect to this important matter judging from the number of complaints I have had, if no assurance can be given that the trouble will be remedied I fear it will mean that a good deal of canning and preserving will not be done this year. I should like to emphasize the importance of that to the parliamentary assistant, and if he can give any assurance I would certainly appreciate it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will be very brief. This
is a most important matter and has been receiving constant attention both by the board and by the Department of Munitions and Supply. As the committee knows, since Pearl Harbor one of the most critical materials has been rubber. Every effort has been made to conserve this very important commodity. The technical officers of the Department of Munitions and Supply, the Department of Agriculture, the wartime prices and trade board and the national reasearch council have all been looking into the question, and I am advised that several months ago they developed specifications which it is believed will provide satisfactory rings.
Are you sure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We are not sure. You can never be sure about anything. I asked my wife about this situation and she told me that last year we put up a good many jars of preserves and vegetables. Perhaps owing to her skill as a preserver none of them turned bad. She used the ordinary rings which were available. All I can say to the committee is that the problem is receiving the earnest attention

both of the Department of Munitions and Supply and of the board, and it is hoped that the rings which will be available this year will be satisfactory. Incidentally it has been decided that synthetic rubber is not suitable for these jar rings, and the very highest grade of reclaimed rubber is being used.

May I ask what happens in
the case of a partnership of two men who have been in business when one buys out the other. The one who retains the business is all right, but what happens to the other fellow, if he wants to enter into business again?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He can get a permit to enter business, as I explained to the hon. member for Bow River.
But he would not have a quota.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the business were one dealing with something in short supply he would have to take his chance on getting a quota. The partner who continued in business would retain the quota that went with that business.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to deal with an item related to wartime prices and trade board order No. 223, which is an order respecting the distribution and use of print paper within Canada. I may point out that earlier this evening charges were hurled back and forth across the floor that members were indulging in partisan political debate. Before anyone makes any charge of that kind may I say quite frankly that I am going to speak briefly about a matter that has special reference to a political party. There is, of course, only one party that I would speak about. The Manitoba section of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, like a number of other sections of our party, publishes a paper. It is called the Manitoba Commonwealth. I have copies of it in my hand.
One thing is clear. This is a political paper and has been from its start. Its whole aim is to educate the people of Canada as to the superiority of the policies of the C.C.F. On May 16 of this year the director of publishing, of the Publishing, Printing and Allied Industries Administration, Mr. F. F. Macnab, wrote to Mr. Lloyd Stinson, editor of the Manitoba Commonwealth at 411 Confederation Life building, Winnipeg, Manitoba, informing him that during 1943 this paper had over-used its quota and that until some proposal came forward from the editor as to how this overuse was to be made good, permit would be withheld for the Manitoba C.C.F. to continue the publication of its paper. Mr. Stinson, the editor, and Manitoba C.C.F. provincial secre-

War Appropriation-Finance
tary, wrote back to Mr. Macnab on May 19 and sent me copies of the correspondence, following which I wrote to Mr. Macnab under date of May 27. I have not had a reply as yet, but I am not complaining unduly of that because there has not been a great deal of time.- I rise to bring the matter up to-night because, if I do not do so on this item and the matter is not dealt with satisfactorily, I shall not have another opportunity to do so.
May I point out to the parliamentary assistant that order 223 as a matter of fact may be a little over-generous. I am not complaining about the order at all. But its terms are such that there should be no restriction on paper for this publication because section 4 (b) reads as follows:
4. This order shall not apply to
(b) any newspaper or other periodical which, in the opinion of the administrator, is published by any religious, charitable^ philanthropic, educational, scientific, professional, political, labour or other non-profit organization.
I point out that the paper is published- and this is very clear from its masthead-by a political party, the Manitoba section of the C.C.F.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What about the proviso? My hon. friend appreciates that, "provided always that the exemptions granted," and so forth.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I will read the proviso:
Provided always that the exemptions granted by this section shall not apply to any newspaper or other periodical that is published primarily for advertiseing purposes, or derives its principal earned revenue from advertising.
The proviso does not affect this paper because it is not published primarily for advertising purposes, nor does it derive its principal revenue from advertising, but from subscriptions and from donations of members of the party to sustain the publication of the paper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If those facts are as stated I am advised that the newspaper will receive a certificate of exemption under this section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that. We were aware of the fact that other political parties seemed to get increased quotas of paper. The paper known as Public Opinion, for instance-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is the quality of that paper that gives it a preference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I may say to the leader of the opposition that it is partly because of the tremendous amount of advertising which Public Opinion has given to the C.C.F. that
there has been an increase in our subscriptions and we need more paper to meet that increase. The increase is due to the advertising which has been given to the C.C.F. not only by Public Opinion but also by the circulation of the Saskatchewan Liberal. These papers are giving the C.C.F. so much publicity that our circulation has increased, and that is the reason for the requirement of extra paper. I am very glad indeed to have the assurance of the parliamentary assistant that there will be no difficulty about getting it. I was sure that there must have been a mistake.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, $140,000,000.

When the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were before the committee there was brought to his attention the subsidy that was supposed to have been paid on potatoes, and I think that matter should be brought up on this item. I have received a number of communications from the potato growing sections of New Brunswick which I visited last fall, and I have in my files a number of newspaper clippings pointing out that there was supposed to have been a subsidy paid by this corporation on early potatoes.
The information I have is that one dealer in this particular part of the province, and one private grower at least, received subsidies on the quantities of potatoes that they shipped out in July and August. I have information that one of the shippers distributed the subsidy to his growers and that this ran anywhere from $90 to $1,000. Apparently he is about the only shipper who took advantage of that, or took advantage in time to get a subsidy. Then something happened, and other growers and shippers have been unable to get that subsidy. The row which has developed over that is that, according to my information, the enterprising shipper who took advantage of the situation and secured the subsidy was a former Liberal candidate. That has raised considerable political turmoil. I think the parliamentary assistant should give us some information as to what the situation is.

I think that, with a corporation such as this, spending so large an amount of money from the treasury, we should have a full and complete report from the minister. I should also be glad if he would bring the financial statement of this Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation up to date as to the operations. Has he the figures
Privilege-Mr. Pouliot

with respect to the operations of this company, we will say to the end of the last financial year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
On the point just raised by . my hon. friend, I had not anticipated that we would be fortunate enough to reach the estimates of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation this evening. However, we have done so. It is five minutes to eleven. I expected to have the officers of the corporation on the floor in front of me in order to assist me in explaining some of these figures. Perhaps in the circumstances the committee would be willing to call it eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Ralston the house adjourned at eleven o'clock until Thursday at four o'clock p.m.
